articles.body_html:
Our order can now wait for a shipping inquiry without pretending that shipping has already succeeded.

The request receives an identifier. The order enters CHECKING_SHIPPING. A matching response may move it to READY_TO_SHIP, while a timeout or unsuccessful result returns it to PAID.

But Part V ended with another requirement:

Before proceeding, the system must obtain both a carrier response and an inventory result.

Those operations may finish in either order.

The carrier might answer first. The inventory system might answer first. One might fail while the other is still working.

How do we combine their results without depending on a particular sequence?

Start with the smallest solution

We could simply perform the checks one after another:

carrier_available = await check_carrier(request)

if carrier_available:
    inventory_available = await check_inventory(request)

This is a reasonable design.

It has an obvious execution order. If the carrier rejects the destination, we avoid the inventory lookup entirely. There is little coordination logic to maintain.

We should preserve that option when the work is cheap, the second operation depends on the first, or avoiding unnecessary requests matters more than overlapping their execution.

But suppose both checks can begin from information we already possess. Neither needs the other’s result.

The serial implementation imposes a dependency that the business rule does not require:

Carrier finishes
        ↓
Inventory may begin

What we actually require is different:

Carrier succeeds
        +
Inventory succeeds
        ↓
The combined check succeeds

Both must finish successfully. Neither must finish first.

Separate checking inventory from reserving it

Before introducing concurrent execution, we need to settle what the inventory operation does.

Checking whether stock is available is not the same as reserving it.

Operation What it establishes
Check inventory The inventory service reports whether the order’s items are currently available.
Reserve inventory The inventory service commits stock to this order under its reservation policy.
Release inventory The service removes an earlier reservation.

The end of Part V raised inventory reservation as a future requirement. We will reach its failure consequences later in this part.

First, we will implement two read-only availability checks. Neither books a shipment nor reserves stock.

This lets us establish the coordination rule without quietly introducing external changes that would need to be undone.

Our inventory adapter will look up the order’s item requirements using its identifier. We are not adding an item model in this lesson. As with the destination in Part V, those requirements remain fixed during one check.

READY_TO_SHIP therefore remains a state in our local simulation. It does not promise that stock is reserved or that carrier capacity will remain available indefinitely.

Fork the work, then join the results

Starting independent branches from one request is commonly described as a fork. Combining their results before continuing is a join.

Our intended flow is:

                    Shipping check
                          │
                         fork
                     ┌────┴────┐
                     ▼         ▼
                 Carrier    Inventory
                  check       check
                     │         │
                     └────┬────┘
                         join
                          │
                          ▼
                  Combined result

The join is not simply the point where two lines meet in a diagram.

It must answer a precise question:

Have all the required branches for this particular request succeeded?

These are two valid execution sequences:

First result Second result Combined outcome
Carrier available Inventory available Available
Inventory available Carrier available Available

After the first successful result, the combined answer is still incomplete.

Starting both operations is not enough. Finishing either operation is not enough.

Readiness requires a successful result from every required branch of the current check.

Why a completion counter is insufficient

We might begin with:

completed_checks = 0

Then increment it whenever a successful result arrives:

completed_checks += 1

if completed_checks == 2:
    report_available()

Now deliver these messages:

Carrier available
Carrier available again

The counter reaches two.

The inventory system has not answered.

We counted messages when the rule required distinct prerequisites.

A duplicate result must not satisfy another branch’s obligation. We need to remember which branch answered, not merely how many messages arrived.

We also need to retain the request identifier from Part V. A carrier answer from yesterday must not combine with an inventory answer for today’s request.

The group of results belongs to:

order identifier
+
check request identifier

Within that group, each result belongs to a named branch.

This is the coordination problem described by the Aggregator pattern in Enterprise Integration Patterns: collect related messages, determine when enough information has arrived, and produce one combined result. The pattern separates correlation, completeness, and the rule used to combine results.[2]

For our case, those decisions are:

Keep the order’s lifecycle intact

We do not need to expose every partial combination as another OrderState.

The order can remain in:

CHECKING_SHIPPING

while a smaller coordination component tracks the branch results.

This preserves the lifecycle from Part V:

PAID
    ↓ CHECK_SHIPPING
CHECKING_SHIPPING
    ↓ combined positive result
READY_TO_SHIP
    ↓ SHIP_ORDER
SHIPPED

The meaning of the positive result is now broader.

Previously, SHIPPING_AVAILABLE meant that the carrier inquiry succeeded. In this version, it means that both required availability checks succeeded.

That is an intentional change in the operation’s contract. A raw carrier response must no longer go directly to the order as SHIPPING_AVAILABLE. It must first pass through the component that combines the results.

The outer ShippingCheckResult envelope can remain unchanged:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ShippingCheckResult:
    order_id: str
    request_id: str
    event: OrderEvent

The order receives one combined answer through the same interface.

Partial progress belongs inside the check, not in the order’s public lifecycle vocabulary.

Give branch results their own vocabulary

Let’s distinguish where a reply came from and what it reports:

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from enum import Enum


class CheckBranch(Enum):
    CARRIER = "carrier"
    INVENTORY = "inventory"


class CheckOutcome(Enum):
    AVAILABLE = "available"
    UNAVAILABLE = "unavailable"
    FAILED = "failed"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BranchResult:
    order_id: str
    request_id: str
    branch: CheckBranch
    outcome: CheckOutcome

UNAVAILABLE means that the lookup completed and returned a negative answer.

FAILED means that an expected service failure prevented us from obtaining an answer.

Those outcomes both prevent readiness under our current policy, but they do not say the same thing.

We can now retain partial progress:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CheckProgress:
    request: ShippingCheck
    carrier: CheckOutcome | None = None
    inventory: CheckOutcome | None = None
    conclusion: OrderEvent | None = None

The existing ShippingCheck contains the order identifier, request identifier, and copied delivery address.

The two branch fields initially contain None, meaning no result has been accepted for that branch.

conclusion is also initially absent. Once set, this check is closed.

For example:

request = check-A
carrier = AVAILABLE
inventory = None
conclusion = None

means that one prerequisite has succeeded and the check is still waiting.

This is not “half an order transition.” It is a complete, valid configuration of the coordination process.

Decide what failure means before writing the handler

There are several reasonable completion policies.

We could wait for every result, even after one branch fails. That would collect more diagnostic information.

We could stop once success becomes impossible. That would avoid waiting for an answer that can no longer change the overall decision.

For these read-only checks, we will choose the second policy:

Accepted branch result Coordinator action
First positive result Record it and continue waiting
Second distinct positive result Conclude SHIPPING_AVAILABLE
Any negative result Conclude SHIPPING_UNAVAILABLE
Any expected lookup failure Conclude SHIPPING_CHECK_FAILED
Duplicate of an accepted result Do not count it again
Result for another request Do not apply it

Once a conclusion exists, later replies cannot reopen the check.

If different failures compete, the first decisive result processed by the coordinator determines the reported outcome. This is an ordering policy, not a claim that the same failure detail will win under every possible schedule.

For successful checks, however, the completion order must not matter.

Apply one branch result at a time

The following function receives the current progress and one reply. It returns updated progress and, only when the check first concludes, a combined result.

def accept_branch_result(
    progress: CheckProgress,
    reply: BranchResult,
) -> tuple[CheckProgress, ShippingCheckResult | None]:
    request = progress.request

    if reply.order_id != request.order_id:
        raise ValueError(
            "Result belongs to a different order."
        )

    if not isinstance(reply.branch, CheckBranch):
        raise TypeError("Unknown check branch.")

    if not isinstance(reply.outcome, CheckOutcome):
        raise TypeError("Unknown check outcome.")

    if reply.request_id != request.request_id:
        return progress, None

    if progress.conclusion is not None:
        return progress, None

    previous = (
        progress.carrier
        if reply.branch is CheckBranch.CARRIER
        else progress.inventory
    )

    if previous is not None:
        if previous is not reply.outcome:
            raise ValueError(
                "Conflicting result for one branch."
            )

        return progress, None

    if reply.branch is CheckBranch.CARRIER:
        updated = replace(
            progress,
            carrier=reply.outcome,
        )
    else:
        updated = replace(
            progress,
            inventory=reply.outcome,
        )

    if reply.outcome is CheckOutcome.FAILED:
        event = OrderEvent.SHIPPING_CHECK_FAILED

    elif reply.outcome is CheckOutcome.UNAVAILABLE:
        event = OrderEvent.SHIPPING_UNAVAILABLE

    elif (
        updated.carrier is CheckOutcome.AVAILABLE
        and updated.inventory is CheckOutcome.AVAILABLE
    ):
        event = OrderEvent.SHIPPING_AVAILABLE

    else:
        return updated, None

    updated = replace(updated, conclusion=event)

    return updated, ShippingCheckResult(
        order_id=request.order_id,
        request_id=request.request_id,
        event=event,
    )

The function does not call either service. It does not change the order. It calculates the consequence of receiving one result.

An identical duplicate leaves progress unchanged.

A contradictory second answer for an already recorded branch raises an error while the group is still open. Our protocol expects one final answer per branch. It does not support silently revising an earlier answer.

After the group closes, subsequent replies are irrelevant to its decision. A production diagnostic path could still record them, but they cannot authorize another transition.

We now have a small stateful process inside the larger workflow.

Its control condition is whether it has concluded. Its supporting data identifies the request and the accepted branch outcomes.

Test the join without relying on task scheduling

Let’s construct a request and its two successful replies:

request = ShippingCheck(
    order_id="order-66",
    request_id="check-A",
    delivery_address="Istanbul",
)

carrier_available = BranchResult(
    order_id=request.order_id,
    request_id=request.request_id,
    branch=CheckBranch.CARRIER,
    outcome=CheckOutcome.AVAILABLE,
)

inventory_available = replace(
    carrier_available,
    branch=CheckBranch.INVENTORY,
)

Now test both possible success orders:

for first, second in (
    (carrier_available, inventory_available),
    (inventory_available, carrier_available),
):
    progress = CheckProgress(request)

    progress, result = accept_branch_result(
        progress,
        first,
    )

    assert result is None
    assert progress.conclusion is None

    progress, result = accept_branch_result(
        progress,
        second,
    )

    assert result is not None
    assert result.event is OrderEvent.SHIPPING_AVAILABLE

    closed = progress

    progress, repeated = accept_branch_result(
        progress,
        second,
    )

    assert progress == closed
    assert repeated is None

Neither branch can complete the join alone. Either can complete it when its counterpart has already succeeded.

The last assertions verify another property: a closed check does not produce a second combined result when a reply repeats.

That is a local property of this coordinator instance. It is not an exactly-once delivery guarantee across crashes or restarts.

Now test the counter mistake directly:

progress = CheckProgress(request)

progress, _ = accept_branch_result(
    progress,
    carrier_available,
)

after_first = progress

progress, result = accept_branch_result(
    progress,
    carrier_available,
)

assert progress == after_first
assert progress.inventory is None
assert result is None

Two carrier messages still satisfy only the carrier prerequisite.

An inventory result from an older request must also remain irrelevant:

stale_inventory = replace(
    inventory_available,
    request_id="older-check",
)

progress, result = accept_branch_result(
    progress,
    stale_inventory,
)

assert progress == after_first
assert progress.inventory is None
assert result is None

Finally, a negative answer closes the current check:

inventory_unavailable = replace(
    inventory_available,
    outcome=CheckOutcome.UNAVAILABLE,
)

progress, result = accept_branch_result(
    progress,
    inventory_unavailable,
)

assert result is not None
assert result.event is OrderEvent.SHIPPING_UNAVAILABLE

If a later positive reply arrives, it does not reverse this conclusion. Starting another inquiry requires a new request identifier and a new CheckProgress.

An older model for independent conditions

Carl Adam Petri’s 1962 dissertation, Kommunikation mit Automaten, investigated the foundations of communication between computational mechanisms.[3]

Petri nets provide a way to model concurrent processes using places, transitions, and tokens. Places describe conditions, tokens mark which conditions currently hold, and transitions consume and produce tokens. The token distribution is called a marking.[4]

The successful path of our check can be sketched as:

                 (check requested)
                         │
                       [fork]
                    ┌────┴────┐
                    ▼         ▼
          (carrier pending) (inventory pending)
                    │         │
          [carrier succeeds] [inventory succeeds]
                    │         │
                    ▼         ▼
           (carrier passed) (inventory passed)
                    └────┬────┘
                       [join]
                         │
                         ▼
                   (checks passed)

Parentheses represent places; brackets represent transitions.

The join requires a token from both successful branches. Firing it consumes those prerequisites and produces the combined completion condition.[4]

This drawing shows only the successful path. Negative results and abandonment need additional paths.

Our Python coordinator is not a general Petri-net engine. But it applies the same useful distinction: independent conditions can become true in either order, while a later action requires their conjunction.

The diagram does not make network calls atomic. It describes when the modeled continuation becomes eligible.

Did we escape state machines?

No.

A bounded set of branch outcomes can still be represented by a finite machine with a state for every combination.

For two branches, that may even be manageable.

The problem is not that a flat FSM is incapable of describing the behavior. The problem is that manually naming every combination makes the independent structure harder to see.

Our representation keeps that structure visible:

Carrier progress
+
Inventory progress
+
Completion rule

The full configuration still has combinations. We have organized them rather than eliminated them.

This is also why the join is more precise than another large lifecycle label. It states which conditions must coexist before the process continues.

Run the branches concurrently without letting them mutate the order

We can now connect the decision logic to asynchronous work.

Python’s TaskGroup starts and owns related tasks, waits for their completion, and propagates unexpected failures. Its task management does not decide whether our business prerequisites passed; that remains the coordinator’s responsibility.[1]

The following executor replaces the single-carrier executor from Part V.

Both adapters receive the immutable ShippingCheck. The carrier adapter uses its destination. The inventory adapter resolves the fixed item requirements using its order identifier.

Expected service failures are translated into AvailabilityLookupError:

import asyncio
from typing import Awaitable, Callable


class AvailabilityLookupError(Exception):
    pass


AvailabilityLookup = Callable[
    [ShippingCheck],
    Awaitable[bool],
]

Now execute and combine the two branches:

async def execute_check(
    request: ShippingCheck,
    carrier: AvailabilityLookup,
    inventory: AvailabilityLookup,
    inbox: asyncio.Queue[ShippingCheckResult],
) -> None:
    progress = CheckProgress(request)

    replies: asyncio.Queue[BranchResult] = (
        asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2)
    )

    async def run_branch(
        branch: CheckBranch,
        lookup: AvailabilityLookup,
    ) -> None:
        try:
            available = await lookup(request)

        except AvailabilityLookupError:
            outcome = CheckOutcome.FAILED

        else:
            if type(available) is not bool:
                raise TypeError(
                    "Availability lookup must return bool."
                )

            outcome = (
                CheckOutcome.AVAILABLE
                if available
                else CheckOutcome.UNAVAILABLE
            )

        await replies.put(
            BranchResult(
                order_id=request.order_id,
                request_id=request.request_id,
                branch=branch,
                outcome=outcome,
            )
        )

    result: ShippingCheckResult | None = None

    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        workers = (
            group.create_task(
                run_branch(CheckBranch.CARRIER, carrier)
            ),
            group.create_task(
                run_branch(CheckBranch.INVENTORY, inventory)
            ),
        )

        while result is None:
            reply = await replies.get()

            try:
                progress, result = accept_branch_result(
                    progress,
                    reply,
                )
            finally:
                replies.task_done()

        for worker in workers:
            if not worker.done():
                worker.cancel()

    await inbox.put(result)

The scheduling callback from Part V now supplies both adapters when it starts this executor.

Neither branch receives the mutable order. Each produces a BranchResult.

One coordinator processes those results sequentially and updates its own local CheckProgress. Only the combined result enters the order’s inbox.

The private queue has room for the two messages these adapters can produce. Its FIFO behavior orders arrivals to this coordinator; it does not impose an order on events in remote services.[5]

We have separated two forms of activity:

External work overlaps. Local decisions about the collected results remain sequential.

A finished task is not necessarily a successful prerequisite

An inventory adapter returning False has completed normally as a Python task.

It has not satisfied the inventory prerequisite.

That distinction is why we translate the return value into an explicit outcome rather than treating task completion as business success.

The executor catches only the expected AvailabilityLookupError. An invalid return type or another programming error is not silently converted into “unavailable.”

On a decisive negative result or expected lookup failure, the coordinator requests cancellation of unfinished sibling tasks. The task group waits for them to finish their cleanup before the executor publishes the combined result.[1]

The adapters must use bounded I/O waits and cooperate with cancellation. A task that blocks the event loop or suppresses cancellation can still delay cleanup.

The task group gives the asynchronous work a lifetime boundary. It does not make arbitrary adapter code reliable.

For a simple case with no need to inspect partial results, a task group followed by an all() check could be enough. Our explicit coordinator earns its place when branch identity, duplicates, stale messages, and early completion rules need to be examined and tested separately.

What happens to the timeout from Part V?

The order’s existing timeout still applies to the entire ShippingCheck.

It is associated with the same request identifier, not separately with “the first branch” or “the second branch.”

Consider:

Step What happens Order behavior
1 Check A begins Enter CHECKING_SHIPPING
2 Carrier A succeeds No aggregate result yet
3 The overall timeout for A is handled Return to PAID
4 Inventory A succeeds Coordinator may produce a result for A
5 That result reaches the order Ignore it because A is no longer outstanding

The outer handler from Part V still checks both the order’s state and the request identifier.

Even a correctly combined result can arrive too late to affect the order.

An overall timeout does not automatically cancel the executor. The surrounding runtime may cancel that task to stop unnecessary work, but the correlation check remains necessary because completion and cancellation can race.

Nor does returning to PAID restore or remove anything in another service. That is safe here because both branches were explicitly defined as read-only inquiries.

We have preserved Part V’s distinction:

Stopping our wait is not proof that remote work stopped.

Both positive replies are not a distributed transaction

Suppose the carrier answers at one moment and inventory answers slightly later.

Our join records two positive observations. It does not prove that both conditions will remain true when another operation eventually tries to book a shipment or reserve stock.

It also does not create one simultaneous snapshot across two services.

For this lesson, the combined result authorizes the next step of our local simulation under the fixed-input assumptions. A production policy might additionally require quotation expiry, inventory holds, or revalidation when committing the real operation.

Those requirements should be introduced explicitly.

Otherwise, the reassuring word READY can claim more than the system actually established.

Now replace the stock check with a reservation

We can now see why the earlier distinction mattered.

Imagine that the inventory branch actually reserves stock:

Inventory reservation succeeds.
Carrier check fails.
The combined operation cannot proceed.

Discarding CheckProgress would not release the reservation.

Cancelling a local task would not necessarily release it either. The inventory service may already have committed the change.

We need another operation:

ReserveInventory
        ↓ later failure
ReleaseReservation

A compensating action counteracts a completed business operation when a larger process cannot finish. It is application-specific, may fail itself, and does not necessarily restore the exact earlier world.[6]

For this example, a release operation would need the reservation identifier. If release fails, the system must retain enough information to continue recovery rather than quietly return to an ordinary state.

An even harder case is:

Reservation succeeds remotely.
Its response is lost.
The local request times out.

Now the system does not know whether a reservation exists.

That requires durable request identity, a way to reconcile the remote outcome, and safe retry or compensation rules. A join condition alone does not supply those mechanisms.

This is why our current executor must not be renamed reserve_inventory without changing its contract and recovery design.

We have implemented concurrent observations. We have not implemented a distributed transaction.

What must remain true as we add more branches?

The code is small, but its correctness depends on several explicit rules.

Each run has one order identifier and one request identifier. Each required branch contributes at most one accepted final result. Success is produced only after every required branch succeeds. A closed run cannot be reopened by a duplicate or late reply.

These rules are independent of which branch happens to finish first.

They also determine what should be tested. Beyond the success permutations, useful cases include a failure before any success, a failure after one success, conflicting replies while a run is open, a reply for another order, and a result arriving after the outer order has timed out.

The runtime tests should separately check that unexpected exceptions propagate and that cancelling the executor cleans up its child tasks. Neither concern should be hidden inside the pure combination logic.

The current implementation still stores its progress in memory. A process crash loses the partial results and the queued output. Producing at most one result during one invocation is not durable exactly-once execution.

That limitation has not changed.

The order and the concurrent work now have different responsibilities

The order’s state machine answers:

Is this combined outcome applicable to the request the order is currently waiting for?

The coordinator answers:

Do the results of the required branches justify producing that combined outcome?

The adapters answer their own service questions.

The coordinator is stateful, but it does not own the order’s lifecycle.

The adapters perform work, but they do not decide when the order becomes ready.

That division keeps independent work from becoming independent mutation of the same record.

But who protects that ownership boundary?

Our order consumer processes its inbox sequentially.

Yet the code that created the mutable Order may still hold a reference to it. Another component could assign its status without sending a message. A queued command could also contain a mutable object that its sender changes after submission.

More queues would not automatically prevent either problem.

We have learned how to collect independent results into one decision. The next problem is making sure that one authority actually controls the state affected by that decision.

When many orders are active, who owns each order’s record, who may change it, and how should every other component communicate with that owner?

References

[1] Python Software Foundation, Coroutines and Tasks. Concurrent task execution, task groups, exception propagation, and cancellation. The example uses APIs available in Python 3.11 and later.

[2] Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, “Aggregator”, Enterprise Integration Patterns. Correlation, completeness conditions, and combining related messages.

[3] Carl Adam Petri, Kommunikation mit Automaten, doctoral dissertation, 1962. University of Hamburg archival record.

[4] Carl Adam Petri and Wolfgang Reisig, “Petri Net”, Scholarpedia, 3(4):6477, 2008. Places, transitions, tokens, and the modeling of concurrent processes.

[5] Python Software Foundation, asyncio Queues. FIFO behavior, bounded queues, and task bookkeeping.

[6] Microsoft, Compensating Transaction Pattern, Azure Architecture Center. Application-specific compensation, recovery information, and failures during compensating work.

articles.body_html:
Last month, I signed up for a hackathon.

I opened a fresh file and named it ideas.md.

Forty-eight hours later, it was still empty.

No meltdown. No rage-quit. Just a blinking cursor and a brain with nothing to give it.

The scary part wasn't the empty file. It was that I couldn't tell you why it was empty.

I used to be the one with too many ideas

There was a version of me with a notes app full of half-built side projects. A version that lost track of time at 1am because the code was fun, not because a deadline said so.

Then life hit me with some personal stuff I didn't see coming. I won't go into the details here, but it knocked me flat.

I stepped away from code. It wasn't really a decision. Survival mode just doesn't leave room for side projects.

When things settled enough, I tried to come back. I figured it'd be like riding a bike.

It wasn't.

  • Hackathons used to feel like a playground. Now they feel like an exam I didn't study for.
  • My feed is full of people shipping, launching and building in public. Meanwhile, I'm struggling to name a variable.
  • Productivity systems? Tried them all. Pomodoro, Notion dashboards, habit trackers. Turns out you can't Pomodoro your way out of feeling empty.
  • Focus comes and goes. I start a tutorial and realize 20 minutes later that nothing went in. I open a tab and forget why.

And underneath all of it, a quiet voice: What if this was never really your thing?

For a long time, I believed it. Whatever I'd had was gone. Deleted. 404 Not Found.

Then I realized I was reading the wrong status code

A 404 Not Found means there's nothing there. You keep asking, and the answer keeps being no.

(Pedants: yes, 410 Gone is technically the "likely permanent" one. But nobody has ever felt a 410 in their soul.)

A 503 Service Unavailable means something completely different. The server is still there. What you're asking for is still there. It just can't handle requests right now.

Here's how the HTTP spec, RFC 9110, describes the cause:

"...a temporary overload or scheduled maintenance, which will likely be alleviated after some delay."

Read that as a sentence about a person, not a server. It might be the most comforting thing I've ever read in a spec.

A 503 can even carry a Retry-After header. That's the server saying not now, try again later. Not goodbye. Just not yet.

None of that describes someone who lost their passion. It describes someone who's been running at 100% CPU through a rough season, with no maintenance window, wondering why every response is slow.

Which made me realize something a little embarrassing:

We'd never run a production server the way we run ourselves.

We give our systems health checks, rate limits, autoscaling and maintenance windows. We give ourselves caffeine and guilt.

So I've started treating myself like a system I actually care about.

What I'm learning (present tense, on purpose)

This isn't a "5 steps to get your passion back" post. Yes, there are five sections. Ignore that.

I don't have this figured out. These are field notes from someone still in the middle of it.

1. Stop retrying in a tight loop

Every dev knows what happens when clients hammer a struggling server with retries: a slowdown becomes an outage. That's why good clients use exponential backoff. Wait, retry, wait longer, retry.

I was doing the exact opposite. Every week I threw something new at myself: another hackathon, another course, another 30-day challenge, another shiny setup. Every time it didn't click, I took it as proof I was broken, and retried harder.

That's not discipline. That's DDoSing yourself from every direction at once.

So I'm letting the queue drain: fewer "shoulds," longer gaps between attempts, and no more treating an off day as a verdict.

Backing off isn't quitting. Rest is part of the protocol.

2. The bug probably isn't in the code

If the database is on fire, refreshing the frontend won't fix it.

My missing spark felt like a coding problem, so I kept trying coding fixes. New stack. New project. New editor theme (not proud of that one).

But the root cause was upstream: sleep, stress, and the personal stuff I'd been pushing down so I could "get back to normal."

Your brain does what your phone does when memory runs low. It kills background apps to keep the essentials running. Creativity, curiosity, the urge to build something just for fun? Background apps. First to go.

That's not a character flaw. It's resource allocation.

So the fix isn't another framework. It's sleep, food, movement, people, and actually dealing with the hard stuff.

And if the hard stuff is heavy, talking to someone (a friend, a therapist, a doctor) isn't weakness. It's reading the logs instead of guessing.

3. Cold starts are slow. That's the spec, not a bug.

If you've deployed a serverless function, you know the cold start. The first request after a long idle is slow and clunky. Nobody looks at a cold start and decides the function is broken forever.

But that's exactly what I did to myself. My first sessions back felt foggy, slow and joyless, and I took that as evidence the spark was dead.

Here's what I'm slowly accepting: motivation is a lagging indicator. I kept waiting to feel it before I started. But the feeling usually shows up after you start, not before.

Psychologists even have a name for working this way, behavioral activation: act first, and let the feeling catch up.

You don't wait for the instance to warm up before you send requests. The requests are what warm it up.

4. Send pings, not payloads

When a server is struggling, you don't send it your heaviest request.

But that's what I kept asking of myself. "Come up with something innovative for this hackathon." "Build a portfolio-worthy side project." "Start a 100-day streak."

That's a 50MB payload aimed at a server that can barely answer a ping. So now I'm sending pings:

  • Fix one tiny bug in an old project.
  • Rebuild something I've built before, with zero pressure for it to be new.
  • Write a 20-line script whose only job is to make me smile. (Free idea: a CLI that roasts your commit messages.)
  • Read someone else's code instead of writing my own.
  • Stop after 25 minutes, even when it's going well. Leave something for tomorrow.

Small. Finishable. Low stakes. The goal isn't productivity. It's a 200 OK.

Every successful response tells the system it's safe to take a little more load.

5. Ideas don't come from blank files

I used to think creative people had some magic idea generator. They don't. They're just noticing things.

Ideas come from input. When you're depleted, there's nothing to remix, so of course ideas.md stays empty. Garbage in, garbage out. Nothing in, nothing out.

What I'm trying:

  • An annoyances log. Every time something irritates me, I write it down: an app that needs six clicks for one thing, a task I do by hand every week, a tool that's almost right. No pressure to build any of it. Every annoyance is a feature request from real life.
  • Building for an audience of one. Forget "innovative." Solve your tiny problem. Git exists because Linus Torvalds needed version control for his own project. No pressure.
  • Consuming on purpose. Read a weird repo. Watch someone code live. Read an outage postmortem. Let other people's ideas bump into yours.

Next hackathon, I'm not walking in with a blank ideas.md. I'm walking in with my annoyances log.

Current status

If I had a status page, here's what it would say right now:

STATUS: DEGRADED PERFORMANCE

[x] Investigating   It's a 503, not a 404
[x] Identified      Overload. Not a skill issue.
[~] Monitoring      Sending pings, backing off when needed
[ ] Resolved        Not yet

"Not yet" is a lot better than "never."

I don't know exactly when the spark comes back. Maybe it'll look different: less fireworks, more embers. I'm starting to think that's fine.

Passion was never supposed to be a hard dependency. Curiosity is enough to start with. Some days, showing up is enough.

For what it's worth, publishing this post is the first 200 OK I've returned in a long time.

HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Retry-After: 86400
X-Still-Here: true

86,400 seconds is one day.

Try again tomorrow. That's the whole plan.

If you've been here and found your way back: what was the first small thing that actually worked? Drop it in the comments. Someone is going to find this post at 2am, and your answer might matter more than everything I just wrote.

And if you're in it right now, just comment 503.

You don't have to explain anything. We'll know.

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

The report was supposed to arrive yesterday. Somewhere in last week's notes, someone said they would send it. Before asking for an update, a researcher has to reconstruct the conversation: who offered, what they offered, and whether there was actually a deadline.

That is the fictional situation in my explicitly synthetic demo. It captures a familiar kind of work: remembering the small agreements that never became formal tasks.

I built PromiseKeeper to turn those agreements into a queue a person can check. Import meeting notes, a chat transcript, or a text file. A local language model proposes commitments. Every suggestion stays beside the exact words that support it. The reviewer can approve it, correct it, dismiss it, or mark it complete.

An approved promise can then become a polite follow-up draft. The person reviews and edits the wording, and decides whether to send it. PromiseKeeper has no sending integration.

The app is built around the difference between a possible promise and a confirmed one. “I'll send the report” deserves attention. “I already sent the report” describes something finished. “If the samples clear, I'll upload the appendix” carries a condition that should stay attached. An uncertain date should remain uncertain.

The interface gives those distinctions room: an evidence review inbox, upcoming and overdue summaries, a timeline, follow-up drafts, and local privacy controls. It supports pasted text and .txt or .md files. SQLite stores the sources and review decisions on the same machine as the local model.

The desired payoff is modest and concrete: bring the relevant promise back into view, with enough context to decide the next step.

I designed the workspace around reading and deciding: a left sidebar, vertically arranged input fields, and charcoal, forest-green and mint surfaces. Source quotes stay readable inside each card. The mobile drawer supports keyboard focus and Escape, and the help dialog explains the review boundary. Follow-up drafts can be copied or downloaded; source deletion lets the person check exactly what they are removing.

Demo

Watch the demo on YouTube. The redesigned interface is demonstrated in a 112.36-second, 1920x1080 recording narrated by genuine Kokoro-82M using af_sarah. The local export is saved at demo/assets/video/final_demo.mp4.

The recording follows a researcher importing five snippets of synthetic notes. Actual local Qwen inference finds three candidates: a revised field report, cleaned survey figures, and a conditional appendix. The already-delivered consent forms and vague conference thought stay out of the action queue.

The reviewer checks the quotes, approves the report, and sees one confirmed promise past its date. Two suggestions remain available for review.

The final action is preparing an editable follow-up. The draft asks whether the recorded timing has shifted; it does not assume the person has failed to deliver.

These are screenshots of the working application. The video preserves the browser's original action timing, with added scene holds for narration. Its edited runtime is not a processing benchmark.

Code

Browse PromiseKeeper on GitHub. The repository includes the frontend, backend, synthetic evaluation corpus, API tests, browser smoke test, real application screenshots, and recording and narration scripts. The recording and narration scripts reproduce the demo; generated video and WAV files are local outputs.

The code is MIT licensed. The selected Qwen model and Kokoro weights have their own licenses and are downloaded separately.

The manual setup uses Python 3.12+, Node 22+, and Ollama. Pull qwen3:8b, start the FastAPI service on port 9000, and run the Next.js frontend. The README contains the commands and a Docker Compose option. There is no paid inference service to configure.

Useful places to begin reading are backend/app/main.py for the extraction and review boundary, app/page.tsx for the user journey, and backend/eval/run_evaluation.py for the measured synthetic evaluation. demo/record_demo.ts and demo/narrate_demo.py reproduce the screen recording and voiceover.

How I Built It

The frontend uses Next.js and TypeScript. FastAPI handles import, local inference, validation, review updates, drafting, export and source deletion. SQLAlchemy stores the relationships in SQLite.

The processing path is small enough to inspect:

Notes → source document and paragraph fragments
      → local Ollama / Qwen extraction
      → schema validation and source-quote check
      → evidence-linked suggestions in SQLite
      → human review → approved promise → editable draft

The configured extractor is Qwen3 8B through Ollama. The locally inspected model reports 8.2 billion parameters and Q4_K_M quantization. The evaluation records the model digest, rather than relying only on a tag that could later point to different weights. Structured extraction runs at temperature zero with reasoning disabled.

The model proposes an action, owner, recipient, deadline, condition, certainty, evidence quote and next step. Pydantic checks the shape of those values. The API then independently verifies that each evidence quote is a literal substring of the original source text. A plausible quote that does not occur in the notes is rejected.

That boundary is useful, but deliberately limited. A quote can be present and still fail to support the proposed owner or claim. The source check establishes provenance; the reviewer still has to establish meaning. The interface keeps the quote beside the action so that check can happen where the decision is made.

The backend also applies conservative lexical rejection to obvious refusals, completed actions and hypothetical statements. An earlier development run exposed false positives in these cases. The final measurements therefore describe the combined prompt, model, schema checks and filters. They are not a score for the base model alone.

Dates need a similar distinction. Explicit dates can be stored directly. Relative timing can be interpreted only when a source timestamp is known. Without that anchor, the date stays unresolved. A missing owner is allowed to remain missing too; filling a field with a confident guess would make the queue less trustworthy.

Each source is split into paragraph fragments with character offsets. Evidence records preserve quotes and their locations. When the same extraction key repeats within an import, the API groups it while retaining distinct supporting quotes. This is normalized exact grouping, not semantic deduplication. Two differently phrased obligations can remain separate, and exact grouping has its own limits when conditions differ. Broader similarity matching needs more work before it should alter a person's action queue.

Review changes create audit events. A source deletion removes its linked commitments and drafts. The dashboard counts confirmed overdue items, and CSV export includes approved commitments with their evidence. The prototype is intended for a person's local machine; shared hosting, account permissions and encrypted storage are separate deployment concerns.

Follow-up drafting uses a deterministic template assembled from approved fields. It does not ask a second model to invent background context, recipients, or excuses. The local model's core job is finding candidate obligations in unstructured conversation. Once the person approves the fields, predictable drafting keeps the next step inspectable.

I checked the implementation with four backend API tests and a production build including TypeScript checks. The browser journey uses genuine local Qwen inference and covers file loading, quote inspection, owner/date/note edits, approval, editable draft copy and download, the timeline, CSV export, completion, source deletion and cancellation, help, mobile keyboard navigation and dark mode. A later import is checked to ensure it does not inherit the previous source timestamp. Automated axe checks report zero violations for the selected rules across 16 light/dark page, dialog and mobile-drawer states; that is a scoped automated check, not a complete manual accessibility audit. The recording runs the actual browser, backend and local model.

For extraction, I authored 55 labelled synthetic cases across 11 categories. The preserved run produced these results:

Check Measured result
Case-level commitment classification 40 true positives, 0 false positives, 0 false negatives
Owner exact match 30 of 35 eligible cases
Explicit calendar-date exact match 5 of 5 eligible cases
Accepted quote substring check 41 of 41 accepted candidate quotes

The owner result is the most useful warning in that table: the system can identify a possible obligation and still attribute it incorrectly. In this corpus, implicit-owner examples account for the five owner mismatches.

The perfect classification result is a small development-set observation. These cases are authored, repetitive, and were used while improving the pipeline. Quote validity is also an enforced acceptance rule, so its perfect rate is not independent evidence of understanding. The evaluation does not score claim entailment and does not cover sarcasm, multilingual conversations, noisy transcription, contradictions, or the full range of date language. The five date examples are a narrow check.

The corpus, evaluator and per-case outputs are preserved so a reader can inspect those limits and add harder examples. Real conversations and a held-out evaluation would be the next useful evidence.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A commitment assistant handles information that can be mundane in isolation and sensitive in combination: who is waiting for whom, which deadline is slipping, and what people agreed to in a private discussion.

Running an open-weight extractor locally makes the data path understandable. After the model has been downloaded, inference does not need a hosted model account. The notes go from the local app to the configured local Ollama service, and the resulting records stay in SQLite. The demo uses synthetic material, but the architecture is chosen for conversations a person would want to keep private.

Open components also make failure inspectable. I can retain a failing synthetic example, adjust the prompt or acceptance filter, and run the same evaluator again. A model digest, a source quote, and a saved result give someone else something concrete to investigate. They can replace the model adapter and keep the validation and human review boundaries.

There are costs to that choice. An eight-billion-parameter model needs a substantial download and enough memory. Local inference can be slow or unavailable on a particular computer. Initial setup is more work than entering a hosted API key. The UI exposes model availability and processing failures because those constraints affect the user's experience.

The same approach carries into the video. Kokoro runs locally, its selected voice and weight hashes are recorded, and the narration script and caption timings are included. The demonstration can be regenerated from the project instead of depending on an unexplained media asset.

The Lazy Payoff

The visible transformation is five raw snippets becoming three candidate obligations, then one approved overdue report and an editable follow-up. The person makes the important decisions while the app gathers the relevant words into one place.

I have not measured saved hours, fewer missed deadlines, or reduced stress. The synthetic demonstration shows a workflow, and the evaluation measures a narrow extraction task. Neither establishes a productivity improvement for real teams.

The burden I want to reduce is repeatedly reconstructing the same agreement before taking a small, reasonable next step. Sometimes that step is sending a reminder. Sometimes it is noticing a condition and waiting. Sometimes it is rejecting the suggestion because there never was a promise.

Keeping that choice with the person matters as much as finding the sentence. A useful assistant should help us remember what we owe one another, while leaving room for people to explain what changed.

Prize Categories

Overall Slow and Steady challenge entry.

articles.body_html:
“Fixed the bug. All tests pass.”

Great.

Which tests? Did they run? Did they cover the bug—or did the agent change the test until it passed?

A confident completion message is easy to read as proof. But before you merge the changes, you need to understand what actually happened.

Here’s a simple workflow for checking an AI agent’s work without manually repeating every step.

1. Define “done” before it starts

“Fix the checkout bug” leaves too much open to interpretation.

Give the agent an observable outcome:

When a discount exceeds the order subtotal, the total should be zero. Add a regression test. Preserve valid discount behavior.

Now you have something concrete to verify.

For a UI task, describe the interaction. For an API task, specify the response and side effects.

Clear acceptance criteria make both implementation and verification easier.

2. Ask for evidence in the completion report

A useful report should include:

  • What changed.
  • Which commands ran.
  • Whether they passed or failed.
  • What could not be checked.

Compare these two reports:

“Everything works.”

And:

“Added a regression test for excessive discounts. The checkout test suite passed. Browser checkout was not tested because payment credentials were unavailable.”

The second report tells you what you can rely on and what still needs attention.

When your tool exposes execution logs, inspect them. A command mentioned in a summary is still a claim until you can confirm its execution.

3. Make sure the test catches the original bug

A passing test is useful only if it checks the behavior you care about.

Suppose the task is to prevent negative totals.

This assertion tells you almost nothing:

expect(result).toBeDefined();

This one checks the requirement:

expect(calculateTotal(50, 80)).toBe(0);

Where practical, confirm that the regression test fails against the original implementation and passes after the fix.

Then check nearby behavior:

expect(calculateTotal(50, 20)).toBe(30);

The goal is to demonstrate that the bug was fixed while preserving expected behavior.

4. Read changes to the tests themselves

Sometimes the implementation needs to change. Sometimes an outdated test needs to change too.

But a green result deserves closer inspection if the agent also:

  • Skipped a failing test.
  • Removed an important assertion.
  • Replaced realistic behavior with a convenient mock.
  • Changed the expected result to match the implementation.
  • Disabled a check in configuration.

These changes can have valid reasons. Ask for the reason and compare it with the requirement.

“Tests pass” has limited meaning if the relevant checks were weakened.

5. Match verification to the change

Different changes need different evidence.

Change Useful verification
Calculation Expected values and boundary cases
API endpoint Status, response body, permissions, and stored changes
Database migration Apply it to representative data and check compatibility
UI interaction Run the interaction and inspect the resulting state
Background job Check retries, duplicate handling, and failure behavior

A successful build proves that the build completed. It doesn’t prove that checkout works.

A screenshot shows appearance. It doesn’t prove that the button saves anything.

Choose checks that exercise the promised behavior.

6. Look for fixes that moved the problem

A small bug can lead to a surprisingly large patch.

Before merging, ask:

  • Did the agent change unrelated files?
  • Did it introduce a dependency for a small task?
  • Did it suppress an error instead of handling it?
  • Did it remove validation to make the request succeed?
  • Did it change a shared function and miss its other callers?

Start with the diff summary, then inspect the affected paths.

A large change isn’t automatically wrong. It should have an explanation proportional to its scope.

7. Treat blocked verification as unfinished verification

Sometimes the agent cannot run a check.

The database is unavailable. A dependency cannot be installed. Browser access is missing.

That is useful information.

The report should say:

“Implemented the change, but integration tests could not run because the test database was unavailable.”

Avoid turning “could not test” into “probably works.”

Record the missing check and complete it in the appropriate environment before relying on the result.

A prompt you can reuse

Add this to your next coding task:

Before editing, state the expected behavior and how you will verify it.

After editing, report:

  1. What changed.
  2. The exact checks you ran and their results.
  3. Whether the regression test catches the original failure, if applicable.
  4. Any tests or checks you changed, removed, or skipped—and why.
  5. What remains unverified.

Only claim a check passed if you actually ran it and observed a passing result.

This won’t eliminate mistakes. It gives you a clearer starting point for assessing the work.

Before you click merge

Ask one question:

“What evidence shows that this change meets the requirement?”

Sometimes the answer is a focused regression test. Sometimes it is an integration run, a browser interaction, or several checks together.

The important part is being able to connect the evidence to the task.

An AI agent can help you implement and verify a change. Its final message should make that verification inspectable.

What’s the biggest gap you’ve found between an agent saying “done” and the work actually being finished?

articles.body_html:
Hardening Webhook Ingestion: Preventing Replay Attacks with Constant-Time HMAC Verification and Idempotency Controls

Public-facing webhook endpoints represent an essential integration surface for modern SaaS platforms and distributed architectures. However, exposing ingestion endpoints to the public internet introduces critical attack vectors, including payload tampering, timing side-channel attacks, and replay attacks.

In this architectural guide, we dissect the design of an enterprise-grade webhook verification pipeline, evaluate an initial Python implementation, analyze a real-world runtime failure caused by dependency management anti-patterns, and establish battle-tested mitigation strategies tailored for production environments.

1. System Architecture and Verification Pipeline Design

To protect downstream services from malicious traffic and resource exhaustion, webhook verification must execute fail-fast validation in strict sequential order. Heavy or stateful operations (such as persistent storage writes or payload deserialization) must only occur after cryptographic integrity is confirmed.

The pipeline implements five sequential validation gates:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as "Third-Party Service"
    participant Pipeline as "WebhookVerifier"
    participant Crypto as "HMAC / Timestamp Validator"
    participant Storage as "State Store (Concurrency Control)"

    Client->>Pipeline: HTTP POST (Raw Body + Signature)
    Pipeline->>Crypto: 1. HMAC-SHA256 Signature Verification
    alt Invalid Signature
        Crypto-->>Pipeline: INVALID_SIGNATURE
        Pipeline-->>Client: 401 Unauthorized
    end

    Pipeline->>Crypto: 2. JSON Deserialization & 3. Schema Validation (Pydantic)
    alt Parse Error / Schema Mismatch
        Crypto-->>Pipeline: MALFORMED_JSON / SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED
        Pipeline-->>Client: 400 Bad Request
    end

    Pipeline->>Crypto: 4. Timestamp Clock Skew Validation
    alt Expired or Out-of-Bounds
        Crypto-->>Pipeline: EXPIRED_TIMESTAMP
        Pipeline-->>Client: 400 Bad Request
    end

    Pipeline->>Storage: 5. Event ID De-duplication (Atomic Lock)
    alt Already Processed (Replay Vector)
        Storage-->>Pipeline: Existing Record Hit
        Pipeline-->>Client: 409 Conflict (or 200 OK for Idempotency)
    else Unprocessed
        Storage-->>Pipeline: Registration Success
        Pipeline-->>Client: 200 OK (Processed)
    end

Core Security Requirements & Technical Rationale

  1. HMAC-SHA256 Signature Verification: To prevent timing side-channel attacks where an adversary infers valid digest bytes through execution duration variance, comparison must be constant-time. We utilize Python's standard hmac.compare_digest to compare the incoming signature with the server-side calculated HMAC across the raw byte payload.
  2. Timestamp Skew Control: Even with valid signatures, an adversary who intercepts an in-flight payload can resend it verbatim unless timestamp boundaries are enforced. By asserting that the request's UNIX epoch timestamp falls within an acceptable tolerance window (e.g., $\pm 300$ seconds), the replay attack window is strictly bounded.
  3. Atomic De-duplication & Idempotency: To defend against replays within the valid time window and handle network retries gracefully, the consumer must track unique event_id identifiers. In multi-threaded or multi-worker systems, cache access must be synchronized using thread locks or distributed atomic operations (e.g., Redis SET NX EX) to prevent race conditions.

2. Implementation Code (Initial Build)

The following implementation translates the five-step pipeline into modular Python components. However, subtle environmental coupling caused this script to fail catastrophically in production:

import hmac
import hashlib
import time
import logging
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any, Tuple
from threading import Lock

import orjson
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

# Structured logging setup
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s'
)
logger = logging.getLogger("WebhookSecurityPipeline")


class WebhookPayload(BaseModel):
    """Schema definition for incoming webhook payloads."""
    event_id: str = Field(..., description="Unique request/event identifier")
    event_type: str = Field(..., description="Classification of the domain event")
    timestamp: int = Field(..., description="UNIX epoch timestamp in seconds")
    data: Dict[str, Any] = Field(default_factory=dict, description="Arbitrary event payload data")


class WebhookSecurityConfig(BaseModel):
    """Configuration governing validation constraints and cryptographic secrets."""
    secret_key: str = Field(..., description="Shared secret key for HMAC verification")
    allowed_skew_seconds: int = Field(default=300, description="Maximum permitted clock drift in seconds")


class WebhookStorageManager:
    """Thread-safe in-memory cache with TTL for event de-duplication."""
    def __init__(self, ttl_seconds: int = 600):
        self._cache: Dict[str, float] = {}
        self._lock = Lock()
        self._ttl = ttl_seconds

    def check_and_mark(self, event_id: str) -> bool:
        """
        Atomically inspect and record an event ID.
        Returns True if the ID was previously processed; False if newly registered.
        """
        with self._lock:
            self._cleanup_expired()
            if event_id in self._cache:
                return True
            self._cache[event_id] = time.time() + self._ttl
            return False

    def _cleanup_expired(self) -> None:
        current_time = time.time()
        expired_keys = [k for k, v in self._cache.items() if v < current_time]
        for k in expired_keys:
            del self._cache[k]


class WebhookVerifier:
    """End-to-end validator for cryptographic verification, parsing, and replay protection."""
    def __init__(self, config: WebhookSecurityConfig, storage: WebhookStorageManager):
        self.config = config
        self.storage = storage

    def verify_signature(self, raw_body: bytes, received_signature: str) -> bool:
        """Constant-time HMAC-SHA256 signature verification."""
        if not received_signature:
            return False

        sig_hash = received_signature
        if received_signature.startswith("sha256="):
            sig_hash = received_signature.split("=", 1)[1]

        computed_mac = hmac.new(
            self.config.secret_key.encode('utf-8'),
            raw_body,
            hashlib.sha256
        ).hexdigest()

        return hmac.compare_digest(computed_mac, sig_hash)

    def verify_timestamp(self, timestamp: int) -> bool:
        """Validates whether the payload timestamp resides within the allowed clock skew window."""
        current_time = int(time.time())
        time_diff = abs(current_time - timestamp)
        return time_diff <= self.config.allowed_skew_seconds

    def process_request(self, raw_body: bytes, received_signature: str) -> Tuple[bool, str, Optional[WebhookPayload]]:
        """
        Orchestrates full-pipeline validation.
        Fails fast upon encountering the first invalid security or schema gate.
        """
        # Step 1: Signature Verification (Constant-Time HMAC)
        if not self.verify_signature(raw_body, received_signature):
            logger.warning(
                "Webhook security incident: Invalid signature detected.",
                extra={"signature": received_signature}
            )
            return False, "INVALID_SIGNATURE", None

        # Step 2: JSON Deserialization (utilizing high-throughput orjson parser)
        try:
            parsed_data = orjson.loads(raw_body)
        except orjson.JSONDecodeError as e:
            logger.error(f"Webhook parse error: Malformed JSON. Details: {e}")
            return False, "MALFORMED_JSON", None

        # Step 3: Schema Validation with Pydantic
        try:
            payload = WebhookPayload(**parsed_data)
        except ValidationError as e:
            logger.error(
                "Webhook validation error: Schema mismatch.",
                extra={"validation_errors": e.errors()}
            )
            return False, "SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED", None

        # Step 4: Clock Skew Verification (Bounded Replay Attack Defense)
        if not self.verify_timestamp(payload.timestamp):
            logger.warning(
                "Webhook security incident: Timestamp out of allowed window.",
                extra={
                    "event_id": payload.event_id,
                    "payload_timestamp": payload.timestamp,
                    "server_timestamp": int(time.time()),
                    "allowed_skew": self.config.allowed_skew_seconds
                }
            )
            return False, "EXPIRED_TIMESTAMP", None

        # Step 5: De-duplication Check (Atomic Concurrency Control)
        if self.storage.check_and_mark(payload.event_id):
            logger.warning(
                "Webhook security incident: Duplicate event ID detected (Replay attack vector).",
                extra={"event_id": payload.event_id}
            )
            return False, "DUPLICATE_REQUEST", None

        logger.info(
            "Webhook successfully verified and processed.",
            extra={"event_id": payload.event_id, "event_type": payload.event_type}
        )
        return True, "SUCCESS", payload

3. Post-Mortem: Root-Cause Analysis of Runtime Failure

Stack Trace and Symptoms

Upon initial execution within a standardized container execution harness, the pipeline immediately crashed before binding to any ingress socket:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/phenox/gemini-sandbox/TOAI_Workspace/V2_SandBox/V2_PROD_20261024_034207_test.py", line 8, in <module>
    import orjson
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'orjson'

Architectural Anti-Patterns Identified

  1. Tight Coupling to Third-Party Optimizations (Unchecked Dependencies): While orjson offers exceptional serialization performance in C-accelerated environments, binding it unconditionally at top-level module scope created an implicit runtime prerequisite. The container base image and deployment manifests lacked explicit automation to compile or install the wheel, causing sudden environment drift.
  2. Absence of Resilient Fallbacks (Degraded Operation Failure): High-throughput accelerators should serve as performance optimizations rather than single points of failure. The module neglected defensive importing or abstraction layers, preventing graceful fallback to Python's standard json module when optimized native extensions are unavailable.

4. Key Takeaways and Resilient Engineering Standards

To construct bulletproof webhook ingestion systems across heterogeneous cloud environments, adopt the following engineering disciplines:

  • Graceful Library Degradation: Decouple serialization logic behind an adapter interface. Check for native high-performance libraries (orjson, ujson) inside try-except blocks, defaulting seamlessly to json.loads if dependencies are missing.
  • Deterministic Environment Management: Enforce dependency isolation using locked manifests (pyproject.toml, uv.lock, or poetry.lock) verified via hermetic CI/CD pipelines.
  • Separation of Raw vs. Deserialized Payloads: Always preserve the exact raw byte stream from the HTTP request body for HMAC calculation. Calculating digests over re-encoded or pretty-printed JSON will alter whitespace and key ordering, causing valid requests to fail signature verification.

articles.title: 616 Bytes to Add Up Sixteen Numbers
articles.description: A comma-separated line parsed with string.Split allocates ~616 bytes a call; the span-based Split that yields Range values allocates nothing. I measured both.
articles.body_html:
I was reading an allocation profile for a request handler that parses a line of comma-separated numbers off an upstream feed. The parse itself is three lines. Nothing in it says new. So I wasn't expecting the fat column of string and string[] allocations sitting right on top of it, climbing every second the feed stayed busy.

They were coming out of one method call: line.Split(',').

Where the bytes come from

Here's the parser, more or less how I'd written it and how I've written it a hundred times before:

static long ParseWithStringSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    foreach (string field in line.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(field, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

Clean, correct, reads like a sentence. The problem is Split. For a line with sixteen fields it hands you back a string[] of length sixteen, and every one of those sixteen entries is a freshly allocated string holding one little number. That's an array plus sixteen substrings on the heap, used for a few microseconds, then dropped on the floor for the GC to sweep up. You call it once at startup and nobody cares. You call it a few thousand times a second and it's a steady drip into gen 0, and gen 0 collections aren't free.

The thing is, I didn't actually want those substrings. I never kept them. I parsed each one into an int and threw the string away. I was allocating sixteen strings purely to look at sixteen slices of a string I already had in my hand.

The span version never makes the substrings

Since .NET 8 there's a split that works directly over a ReadOnlySpan<char> and gives you back Range values instead of strings. You slice into the original span yourself, and int.Parse has taken a span since .NET Core 2.1, so nothing ever gets copied into a new string:

static long ParseWithSpanSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    foreach (Range r in span.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(span[r], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

The logic is identical. The only difference is Range r instead of string field, and span[r] instead of the field. span[r] isn't a copy, it's a window onto the characters already sitting in line. No array, no substrings, nothing for the collector to chase.

I counted it

I don't trust my own intuition about allocations, so I wrote the smallest thing that would show the gap. Same sixteen-field line, both parsers, five million calls each. I read GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around each loop and took the best of seven rounds. Here's the output:

Both parsers sum the line to 7074. Good.

string.Split:  3,080,000,040 bytes,   1657.5 ms  (best of 7)
span Split  :             40 bytes,   1105.2 ms  (best of 7)

Allocated per call: string.Split 616 B, span 0 B
Time ratio (best of 7): span is 1.50x the throughput of string.Split

616 bytes a call to add up sixteen numbers. The span version: a flat 40 bytes for the whole five-million-call run, which rounds to zero per call. That 40 is a one-time constant, not something that scales with the work.

I ran it a few times and the allocation numbers didn't move a single byte, which is what I'd expect since they're structural. The timing wandered between about 1.5x and 1.7x the throughput depending on the round. I'm on a shared two-core container, not a quiet benchmark box, so I trust the allocation figure a lot more than the milliseconds. The honest read is: the span path is clearly faster here, and the real, repeatable win is that it stops allocating entirely.

When I don't bother

I'll say the obvious part out loud, because it's the part that matters more than the benchmark. If your parse runs once when the app boots, 616 bytes is nothing. Don't go rewriting readable code to save a few hundred bytes you allocate at startup and never again. string.Split is clearer, and clearer wins when the perf doesn't matter.

There are real limits to the span split too, and they bit me the first time I reached for it. It splits on every occurrence of the separator, full stop. There's no StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries, no trimming, no cap on the number of pieces. If your input has empty fields you care about skipping, or you want the "split into at most 3" behaviour, you're either back on string.Split or writing that logic by hand. And because a span is a ref struct, this parser has to stay synchronous. You can't stash the span in a field or carry it across an await, so the moment your parsing wants to be async, this shape stops working.

So my rule is narrow on purpose. When the parse is sitting in a loop that runs often and I can see it in a profile, I switch to the span split and the allocations just disappear. Everywhere else I leave string.Split alone, because the only thing I'd be buying is a worse-looking method.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. New console project targeting net10.0, drop this in Program.cs, dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Globalization;

const string line = "1024,37,8,512,9,1,4096,16,64,2,128,256,7,3,900,11";

long expected = ParseWithStringSplit(line);
long actual = ParseWithSpanSplit(line);
if (expected != actual) { Console.Error.WriteLine("Parsers disagree"); return 1; }
Console.WriteLine($"Both parsers sum the line to {expected}. Good.\n");

const int iterations = 5_000_000;
const int rounds = 7;

var (splitBytes, splitMs) = Measure("string.Split", iterations, rounds, ParseWithStringSplit, line);
var (spanBytes, spanMs) = Measure("span Split  ", iterations, rounds, ParseWithSpanSplit, line);

Console.WriteLine($"\nAllocated per call: string.Split {splitBytes / (double)iterations:F0} B, span {spanBytes / (double)iterations:F0} B");
Console.WriteLine($"Time ratio (best of {rounds}): span is {splitMs / spanMs:F2}x the throughput of string.Split");
return 0;

static (long bytes, double ms) Measure(string name, int iterations, int rounds, Func<string, long> parse, string line)
{
    long bestBytes = long.MaxValue;
    double bestMs = double.MaxValue;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++)
    {
        long acc = 0;
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) acc += parse(line);
        sw.Stop();
        long bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
        if (acc == long.MinValue) Console.WriteLine(acc); // keep acc observable
        bestBytes = Math.Min(bestBytes, bytes);
        bestMs = Math.Min(bestMs, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"{name}: {bestBytes,14:N0} bytes, {bestMs,8:F1} ms  (best of {rounds})");
    return (bestBytes, bestMs);
}

static long ParseWithStringSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    foreach (string field in line.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(field, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

static long ParseWithSpanSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    foreach (Range r in span.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(span[r], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

Do you reach for the span split by default, or only after a profiler points at it? I'm curious where other people draw that line.

— still counting bytes nobody asked me to count
