13. Vector Search Security

The vector store holds your most sensitive data in a new form

A vector database stores embeddings derived from your documents, usually alongside the text itself and metadata like ACLs. It is reachable by services that take untrusted input, and it has a query interface that returns "the nearest things to whatever you ask." All the security fundamentals apply (see AI Security); this section covers what is specific to vector stores.

Threats 

CROSS-TENANT / CROSS-USER LEAKAGE   A missing or bypassable filter returns another tenant's or user's content. The #1 vector-store incident class. Includes filtered-ANN edge cases and post-filter shortcuts.
UNAUTHENTICATED OR EXPOSED ENDPOINTS  Vector databases (and their dashboards) bound to public interfaces with no authentication or default credentials — a recurring real-world exposure. Anyone who can query can read.
EXCESSIVE PRIVILEGE                 One credential that can read, write, delete, and administer — so a bug or compromise in the query service can wipe or poison the index.
EMBEDDING INVERSION / DATA RECOVERY Research shows that text can be partially reconstructed from embeddings; vectors alone are NOT anonymized. Treat them as sensitive as the source.
MEMBERSHIP / ATTRIBUTE INFERENCE    Probing nearest neighbors can reveal whether specific content (a person's record, a confidential document) is in the index.
CORPUS POISONING                    An attacker who can add content (a wiki page, an uploaded file, a crawled page) crafts text that embeds close to many queries ("hub" documents) or carries prompt-injection payloads, so it is retrieved
                                    and influences answers (see AI Security, Section 2).
FILTER / QUERY INJECTION            Filters built by concatenating user input into OData, SQL, or JSON filter strings allow filter bypass or errors.
RESOURCE EXHAUSTION                 Huge k, expensive filters, very high efSearch/ef, unbounded batch queries, or rapid-fire requests degrade or take down the index (and run up cost).
EXFILTRATION BY QUERY               An attacker with query access (or via a prompt-injected agent) can systematically scrape the index by issuing many varied queries.
SUPPLY CHAIN                        Compromised client libraries, container images, or models; unreviewed extensions.
BACKUP / SNAPSHOT / LOG EXPOSURE    Snapshots, embedding lakes, and logs/traces containing payloads and queries with weaker access control than the live system.
INSIDER / OVERBROAD ADMIN ACCESS    Operators who can read all tenants' data.

Defenses 

AUTHENTICATION AND NETWORK
  - Never expose a vector store to the public internet. Private endpoints/VNet integration, firewall allow-lists, TLS everywhere. Change default ports/credentials; disable anonymous access and unused dashboards.
  - Prefer identity-based authentication (Entra ID/managed identity) over static keys; if keys are used, store them in a vault, scope them, rotate them (see AI Security, Section 10).

LEAST PRIVILEGE
  - Separate identities for QUERY (read-only, scoped to one index/namespace), INGESTION (write to specific indexes), and ADMIN (schema, deletion, key management). The query service must not be able to delete or reconfigure.
  - Per-tenant scoped credentials where the engine supports them.

ACCESS CONTROL IN THE QUERY, AND AGAIN AT HYDRATION
  - Derive tenant and ACL filters from the authenticated identity on the server and apply them INSIDE the vector query (pre-filter). Never post-filter for security, never take the tenant from the request or the model.
  - Defense in depth: store only IDs (and minimal metadata) in the vector index, and fetch the actual text from an authorized system of record AFTER re-checking the user's permission. A vector-index bug then can't hand out content by itself.
  - Enforce isolation structurally where possible (silo/partition per tenant, row-level security) so a coding mistake is not a breach (Section 8).

INPUT HARDENING
  - Typed filter objects, allow-listed fields and operators; ESCAPE or parameterize any value that must appear in a filter expression; cap k, filter complexity, query size, and ef/probe settings server-side.
  - Rate limit per user/tenant and detect scraping patterns (see AI Security, Section 11).

DATA PROTECTION
  - Encryption in transit and at rest (customer-managed keys where policy demands); encrypt and access-control snapshots and the embedding lake the same as the source.
  - Minimize what the index stores (don't copy sensitive fields into payloads "for convenience"); redact PII before embedding where the use case allows (see AI Security, Section 5).
  - Retention and deletion that actually purges (Section 9).

CORPUS INTEGRITY
  - Control who can write to the index; record provenance (source, author, ingestion time); scan and sanitize ingested content (hidden text, instructions); quarantine suspicious documents; allow rapid removal by source.
  - Treat retrieved text as UNTRUSTED when it reaches a model (delimiting, least-privilege tools — see AI Security, Section 2, and Advanced RAG Architecture, Section 2).
  - Monitor for "hub" documents that appear in an abnormally large share of results.

AUDIT AND DETECTION
  - Log who queried which index with what filters and how many results (metadata, not content); alert on unusual query volume, new filters, bulk reads, access from unexpected locations, and admin operations.
  - Test tenant isolation continuously (Section 8) and run adversarial queries as part of security testing (see AI Security, Section 14).

SUPPLY CHAIN
  - Pin and scan client libraries and images; review extensions; verify model and artifact checksums (see AI Security, Section 12).

A hardened query wrapper 

public sealed class SecureVectorSearch(IVectorIndex index, ILogger<SecureVectorSearch> log)
{
    private const int MaxK = 50;
    private static readonly HashSet<string> AllowedDocTypes = ["policy", "manual", "faq", "runbook"];

    public async Task<IReadOnlyList<Hit>> SearchAsync(UserContext user, float[] queryVector, SearchRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        int k = Math.Clamp(request.Top, 1, MaxK);                                           // cap result size server-side

        // SECURITY filters come from the authenticated identity ONLY. Group IDs should be GUIDs/opaque IDs without commas.
        var clauses = new List<string>
        {
            $"tenantId eq {ODataQuote(user.TenantId.ToString())}",
            $"group_ids/any(g: search.in(g, {ODataQuote(string.Join(",", user.GroupIds))}, ','))"        // the Azure AI Search security-trimming pattern
        };

        // BUSINESS filters are allow-listed and escaped — never concatenated from raw input
        if (request.DocType is not null)
        {
            if (!AllowedDocTypes.Contains(request.DocType)) throw new ArgumentException("Unsupported document type.");
            clauses.Add($"docType eq {ODataQuote(request.DocType)}");
        }

        string filter = string.Join(" and ", clauses);
        IReadOnlyList<Hit> hits = await index.SearchAsync(queryVector, k, filter, ct);       // the filter is applied INSIDE the query (pre-filter)

        // Defense in depth: hydrate text from the system of record, re-checking the user's permission on each item
        var authorized = new List<Hit>();
        foreach (Hit hit in hits)
            if (await documents.UserCanReadAsync(user, hit.DocId, ct)) authorized.Add(hit);

        log.LogInformation("Vector search by {User} tenant {Tenant}: {Returned}/{Requested} authorized", user.Id, user.TenantId, authorized.Count, k);   // metadata only, never query text
        return authorized;
    }

    // OData string literals escape a single quote by doubling it
    private static string ODataQuote(string value) => "'" + value.Replace("'", "''") + "'";
}

Treat embeddings as data subject to the same obligations 

CLASSIFICATION   Vectors inherit the classification of their source (confidential text -> confidential vectors).
RESIDENCY        Where vectors are stored and processed is subject to the same residency rules.
SUBJECT RIGHTS   Access, correction, and erasure requests apply to embeddings and derived payloads (Section 9).
THIRD PARTIES    Hosted embedding APIs and hosted vector databases are data processors: review retention, training use, sub-processors, and regions.
LOGGING          Don't log raw vectors or queries containing sensitive text; redact before capture (see AI Observability, Section 12).

14. Capacity Planning

Do the arithmetic before you buy hardware 

public static class VectorCapacity
{
    private const double GiB = 1024.0 * 1024 * 1024;

    // Raw vector storage: N x dimensions x bytes per dimension
    public static double RawVectorsGiB(long n, int dims, double bytesPerDim) => n * dims * bytesPerDim / GiB;

    // HNSW links: layer 0 holds up to 2*M neighbor IDs per node (4 bytes each), plus a few percent for upper layers and bookkeeping.
    // Real engines add their own overhead (metadata, deleted flags, ID maps); treat this as a floor.
    public static double HnswGraphGiB(long n, int m) => n * (2.0 * m * 4) * 1.10 / GiB;

    // IVF-Flat: full vectors + one list entry per vector + centroids
    public static double IvfFlatGiB(long n, int dims, double bytesPerDim, int nlist) =>
        (n * dims * bytesPerDim + n * 8.0 + (double)nlist * dims * 4) / GiB;

    // Product quantization: m sub-vector codes of `bitsPerCode` bits per vector (excludes the full-precision vectors kept for rescoring)
    public static double PqGiB(long n, int subvectors, int bitsPerCode = 8) => n * subvectors * bitsPerCode / 8.0 / GiB;
}

EXAMPLES (illustrative)
  10 M vectors x 1,536-d float32:    raw vectors 57.2 GiB;   HNSW (M = 16) links ≈ 1.3 GiB   -> the graph is only ~2% on top of the vectors at this dimensionality
  10 M vectors x   128-d float32:    raw vectors  4.8 GiB;   HNSW (M = 16) links ≈ 1.3 GiB   -> ~27%: at LOW dimensionality the graph overhead is significant
  100 M vectors x 1,536-d:           float32 572 GiB   int8 143 GiB   binary / PQ(192 B) 17.9 GiB   (+ full-precision vectors on cheaper storage if rescoring)

REAL-WORLD HEADROOM (multiply the floor by...)
  x 1.5-2.0   for engine overhead, metadata/payload indexes, fragmentation, segment merges, and growth between rebuilds
  x replicas  each replica holds a full copy for availability and read throughput
  + working memory for queries, filters, and (importantly) index builds/rebuilds, which can need substantially more RAM than serving
  + OS page cache so the index stays memory-resident
PLAN CAPACITY FOR NEXT YEAR'S DATA, not today's — rebuilding a full index under pressure is the expensive way to learn you under-provisioned.

Levers that change the arithmetic 

FEWER DIMENSIONS     1,536 -> 768 halves vector memory and per-comparison cost.
SMALLER NUMERIC TYPE float32 -> float16/int8/binary: 2x / 4x / 32x, with rescoring to recover recall.
TIERING              Hot data in RAM at full precision, warm quantized or on disk, cold archived (Section 9).
DEDUPLICATION        Near-duplicate chunks and documents waste vectors (and result slots): deduplicate at ingestion.
CHUNKING CHOICES     Larger chunks (or parent-child indexing of small children only) change vector counts by multiples.
SHARDING             Splits memory across nodes (adds fan-out); does not reduce total memory.

15. Choosing and Operating a Vector Database

Engineering questions that decide the choice 

SCALE AND MEMORY      How many vectors, what dimensions, what growth? Does the engine support quantization and disk-oriented indexes if RAM cost bites?
INDEX TYPES           HNSW only, or also IVF/PQ, flat, and disk-based graphs? Can you tune parameters per index/query?
FILTERING             How does it combine filters with ANN — pre-, post-, or in-graph? Indexed payload fields? Behavior at selective filters (test it)?
HYBRID                Native keyword + vector with fusion? Sparse vectors? Multi-vector fields?
MULTI-TENANCY         What primitives exist (namespaces, partitions, per-tenant shards, per-tenant indexes) and what are the limits?
UPDATES AND DELETES   Real-time upserts? How are deletes handled and compacted? Freshness (write-to-searchable lag)?
CONSISTENCY AND DURABILITY  Replication, snapshots, restore tooling, RPO/RTO.
SECURITY              Identity-based auth, RBAC granularity, private networking, encryption/CMK, audit logs.
OPERATIONS            Managed vs. self-hosted, upgrade story, monitoring/metrics, cost model (per vector, per query/RU, per replica).
ECOSYSTEM             .NET SDK quality, integration with Microsoft.Extensions.VectorData / Semantic Kernel connectors, your existing database or cloud.

A rough feature map (verify against current documentation — these evolve) 

POSTGRESQL + PGVECTOR         HNSW and IVFFlat; halfvec and binary-quantization options; iterative filtered scans; SQL joins, transactions, RLS, partitioning. Strong when vectors belong next to relational data; RAM-bound at very large scale.
AZURE AI SEARCH               HNSW and exhaustive KNN; scalar/binary quantization with rescoring; native hybrid (BM25 + vector, RRF) and semantic ranking; filterable fields and vector filter modes; replicas/partitions scale; managed.
SQL SERVER / AZURE SQL        Native vector data type and distance functions, with approximate (DiskANN-style) vector indexes arriving in recent versions — useful when vectors should live in the relational engine you already run.
AZURE COSMOS DB               Flat, quantized-flat, and DiskANN vector indexes inside a globally distributed document database.
MONGODB ATLAS                 Vector search index over document fields, with filter fields, quantization options, and Atlas Search for hybrid.
REDIS                         In-memory HNSW and FLAT with tag/numeric/text filtering; lowest latency, memory-priced.
ELASTICSEARCH / OPENSEARCH    HNSW alongside mature inverted-index search, filtering, and aggregations; quantization options.
DEDICATED VECTOR DATABASES    Qdrant (payload indexes, named and sparse vectors, quantization), Weaviate (multi-tenancy objects, hybrid), Milvus (many index types incl. disk and GPU, partition keys), Pinecone (managed, namespaces).
Choose the one closest to your existing data and operational skills that passes YOUR benchmark on filtered recall, latency, and cost — then abstract it behind your own interface so the decision stays reversible.

An operating checklist 

DESIGN       Embedding spec recorded; dimensions chosen and justified; metric/normalization documented; tenancy model decided; filter fields indexed; index parameters set explicitly (no silent defaults).
MEASURE      Benchmark queries + exact ground truth; recall@k including filtered; latency percentiles under load; recall canary scheduled in production.
SECURE       Private networking; identity auth; separate read/write/admin identities; tenant/ACL filters inside queries; ID-only index with authorized hydration; input caps and rate limits; encryption; audit logging.
OPERATE      Index health metrics (deleted ratio, merges, freshness); compaction/reindex schedule; backups AND tested restores; embedding lake for rebuilds; documented rebuild runbook with timing.
CHANGE       Blue/green indexes and alias swaps for parameter, model, and engine changes; shadow reads; staged cutover; rollback window.
GOVERN       Retention and erasure procedures covering vectors, payloads, caches, and backups; tenant offboarding verified; cost attribution; capacity forecast for the next 12 months.

16. Interview-Style Questions

Concise model answers — expand with examples from your own experience.

1. Cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance — when do they give the same ranking?
When vectors are normalized to unit length: ‖a−b‖² = 2 − 2·cos(a,b) and dot = cosine, so all three rank neighbors identically. For unnormalized vectors they differ — cosine ignores magnitude, dot product and L2 don't — so use the metric the model was trained for, and prefer dot product on normalized vectors because it's cheapest.

2. What does an HNSW index do, and what do M, efConstruction, and efSearch control?
HNSW is a layered proximity graph: sparse upper layers give long hops, layer 0 holds all vectors; search descends greedily then runs a beam search of width efSearch. M is the number of links per node (recall vs. memory/build time), efConstruction is the build-time candidate width (graph quality vs. build cost), efSearch is the query-time width (recall vs. latency) and is the knob to tune first.

3. HNSW versus IVF — how do you choose?
HNSW generally gives the best recall/latency when the index fits in RAM, builds incrementally, but is memory-heavy, slow to build, and awkward for deletes and filters. IVF (especially with PQ/SQ) is smaller, faster to build, handles deletes and filters naturally, and scales beyond RAM, but needs representative training, drifts, and usually trails HNSW at equal recall. Start with HNSW at RAG scale; consider IVF-PQ or disk-based graphs when memory cost dominates.

4. Why does adding a filter hurt approximate-search recall, and what do you do about it?
The index is built over all vectors; a selective filter removes most candidates from a post-filtered ANN result (too few results) or disconnects the graph traversal. Use pre-filtering with an exact scan when the candidate set is small, filter-during-search with a wider ef when moderate, indexed filter fields, partitions/partial indexes for hot filters like tenant, iterative scans (pgvector 0.8+), and always measure filtered recall at several selectivities.

5. How would you design multi-tenancy for a vector store?
Choose by tenant count and isolation needs: pooled (tenant filter) for many small tenants, partitions/namespaces as a middle path, index per tenant for stronger isolation and per-tenant keys/models, deployment per tenant for regulated customers — often tiered. Enforce isolation structurally (tenant from identity in a repository layer, row-level security or per-tenant credentials), route small tenants to exact search, add noisy-neighbor limits, and test cross-tenant leakage in CI.

6. How do you handle deletes and updates in an ANN index?
Updates are delete + insert; deletes are tombstoned and excluded from results but leave the graph/lists dirty until compaction, vacuum, or reindex, so heavy churn wastes memory and degrades recall. Monitor the deleted ratio, schedule maintenance or rebuild-and-swap, make upserts idempotent and version-checked, and remember soft deletes don't satisfy erasure obligations.

7. How do you migrate to a new embedding model with no downtime?
Treat it as a new vector space: build a new index (or new named vector field) with the new spec, backfill from source or the embedding lake within provider rate limits, evaluate on the benchmark, shadow traffic, switch an alias, keep the old index for rollback, and recalibrate similarity thresholds. Never mix specs in one ANN search; stamp every vector and trace with the embedding spec.

8. How do you migrate between vector engines?
Copy existing vectors and payloads rather than re-embedding; dual-write via change feed, backfill with resumable batched upserts, bulk-load first and index after, verify counts plus search quality (recall vs. exact, overlap@k with the old system), shadow reads, staged cutover, rollback window. Re-verify metric semantics, filter syntax, defaults, hybrid behavior, consistency model, and the security/tenant-isolation implementation on the new engine.

9. A vector query is slow. How do you diagnose and tune it?
Measure first: is time in the embedding call, the search, payload retrieval, or the network? Check that the index fits in memory and is actually used (EXPLAIN), then sweep efSearch/nprobe against exact ground truth to pick the smallest setting meeting the recall target, and consider fewer dimensions, quantization with rescoring, smaller k, fetching payloads only for the final IDs, filter-aware planning, caching, co-location, and replicas for throughput. Always check recall alongside latency.

10. What is quantization with rescoring and why use it?
Compress vectors (int8, binary, PQ) to cut memory 4–32× and speed up approximate scoring, retrieve an oversampled shortlist (3–10× k), then re-score only those with full-precision vectors to recover recall. It makes large indexes affordable; the oversampling factor and quality loss must be measured on your data.

11. What are the security risks specific to a vector database?
Cross-tenant leakage through missing or bypassable filters, exposed unauthenticated endpoints, overbroad credentials, embedding inversion (vectors aren't anonymous), corpus poisoning and prompt injection via retrieved chunks, filter injection, resource exhaustion and scraping via queries, and unprotected snapshots/logs. Mitigate with private networking and identity auth, least-privilege split identities, ACL filters inside the query plus authorized hydration from the system of record, typed/escaped/allow-listed filters, caps and rate limits, encryption, provenance controls, and audit logging.

12. How big will my index be?
Vectors: N × dimensions × bytes per dimension (1M × 1,536 × float32 ≈ 5.7 GiB); HNSW adds roughly 2M×4 bytes per vector for links (small at high dimensions, significant at low); add 1.5–2× for engine overhead and growth, multiply by replicas, and reserve extra working memory for rebuilds. Reduce with fewer dimensions, quantization, and tiering.

13. Why can't you compare vectors from two different embedding models?
Each model defines its own geometry; coordinates and distances have no shared meaning, so cross-model similarity is noise that still returns plausible-looking numbers. That is why the embedding spec (model, version, dimensions, normalization, preprocessing) is stored with every vector and checked at query time.

17. Common Pitfalls

Pitfall Why it hurts Better approach
Querying with a different metric than the index was built for Index unused (full scan) or wrong neighbors Match operator/metric to the index's operator class; normalize on write (Section 2)
Using dot product on unnormalized text embeddings Vector magnitude, not meaning, drives rankings Normalize, or use cosine (Section 2)
Mixing normalized and unnormalized vectors Dot/L2 rankings break silently Enforce and test normalization in ingestion (Section 2)
Assuming more dimensions means better retrieval Higher cost with little or no gain Benchmark smaller dimensions / Matryoshka truncation (Section 1)
Truncating a model not trained for it Large quality loss Truncate only models that support it; re-normalize (Section 1)
Trusting default HNSW/IVF parameters Wrong recall/latency for your data Sweep runtime knobs; rebuild with tuned M/efConstruction if recall plateaus (Sections 4, 12)
Judging an index by unfiltered recall Filtered recall can be far worse Measure recall at several filter selectivities (Section 6)
Post-filtering for access control Too few results and potential leakage Pre-filter inside the query; structural isolation (Sections 6, 13)
Unindexed filter fields Metadata scans dominate latency Declare and index filterable fields (Section 6)
Letting the HNSW index spill out of RAM Latency cliff Size memory with headroom; quantize or shard (Sections 4, 14)
Ignoring tombstones and churn Bloat, slower queries, degraded recall Monitor deleted ratio; schedule compaction/reindex; alias-swap rebuilds (Section 9)
Treating soft delete as erasure Data still stored; compliance failure Hard delete across index, payloads, caches, backups (Section 9)
Dual-writing from application code Index and source diverge on partial failure Outbox/CDC with idempotent, version-checked upserts plus reconciliation (Section 9)
No embedding spec stored with vectors Can't tell what space vectors live in; unsafe migrations Store spec ID per vector and in index metadata; check at query time (Section 10)
Mixing embedding versions in one ANN search Meaningless similarity scores Separate indexes/fields per spec; blue/green cutover (Section 10)
Re-embedding for an engine migration Slow, costly, subtly different vectors Copy existing vectors; use an embedding lake (Sections 9, 11)
Building indexes incrementally during bulk loads Days-long builds Load first, build index after, with tuned build memory/parallelism (Section 11)
Cutting over without comparing search behavior Silent quality regressions Shadow reads, overlap@k, recall vs. exact, filter parity (Section 11)
Tuning latency without watching recall "Faster" because worse Always sweep recall and latency together against exact ground truth (Section 12)
Pulling large payloads for every candidate Slow queries and heavy bandwidth Return IDs from search; hydrate only the final few (Sections 12, 13)
One multi-tenancy model for all tenants Small-tenant recall problems or runaway per-tenant overhead Tiered model; exact search or partitions for small tenants; silo for large/regulated ones (Section 8)
Session-level tenant settings on pooled connections Tenant context leaks into the next request Transaction-local settings (set_config(..., true)) with row-level security (Section 8)
Exposed vector DB ports and dashboards Direct data exposure Private networking, authentication, no anonymous access (Section 13)
Concatenating user input into filter strings Filter bypass and injection Typed filters, allow-lists, escaping (Section 13)
Treating embeddings as anonymous Inversion and inference risks; compliance gaps Classify vectors like their source; same controls, residency, and erasure (Section 13)
No recall canary in production Silent drift after churn, upgrades, or tuning Scheduled exact-ground-truth canary with alerts (Section 12)
Capacity planned for today's data Emergency rebuilds under load Forecast 12 months, include headroom, replicas, and rebuild memory (Section 14)

Quick Reference Table

Topic Key idea Practical takeaway
Dimensions Fixed by the embedding model; cost = d × bytes × N 1,536-d float32 ≈ 6 KiB/vector; test smaller dims (Matryoshka)
Metrics Cosine = dot = L2 ranking on unit vectors Normalize on write; use the model's metric; match index and query metrics
ANN Trade recall for speed and memory Measure recall@k vs. exact on your data; use exact search for small N and tiny filtered sets
HNSW Layered proximity graph Tune efSearch first; M and efConstruction at build; RAM-resident; deletes and filters are hard
IVF k-means cells + nprobe scan Smaller and faster to build; needs training; pairs with PQ/SQ and rescoring
Quantization int8 / binary / PQ compression 4–32× smaller; oversample and rescore with full precision
Filtering Pre-, post-, or in-graph Selectivity decides; exact scan for tiny sets; verify filtered recall; index filter fields
Hybrid indexes Inverted index + ANN (+ sparse/multi-vector) One engine simplifies filters and consistency; fuse by rank (RRF)
Multi-tenancy Pooled, partitioned, silo, deployment-per-tenant Tier by tenant size/isolation needs; enforce structurally; test leakage
Data lifecycle Derived, rebuildable data Idempotent version-checked sync; tombstones; compaction; retention and real erasure; embedding lake
Embedding versioning Spec = model + version + dims + normalization + preprocessing Store spec per vector; blue/green or named vectors; never mix specs
Migrations Move vectors, don't recompute Dual-write, resumable backfill, load-then-index, shadow reads, staged cutover
Performance tuning Measure → change one thing → re-measure recall and latency Memory fit, efSearch/nprobe, dims, quantization, smaller k, caching, replicas
Security Isolation, exposure, inversion, poisoning, injection Private + identity auth, split identities, ACL in query + authorized hydration, typed filters, audit
Capacity N × d × bytes (+ graph + overhead × replicas) Forecast growth; headroom 1.5–2×; rebuild memory

Conclusion

A vector database looks simple from the outside — put vectors in, get neighbors out — but each layer has engineering consequences. Dimensions set memory, bandwidth, and per-query cost, and are one of the cheapest things to shrink. The three similarity metrics collapse into one on normalized vectors, so the practical rules are to normalize on write, use the model's metric, and never query with a metric the index wasn't built for. Approximate search buys speed by giving up some recall: HNSW does it with a layered graph you tune mainly through efSearch (and M and efConstruction at build time), IVF with k-means cells and nprobe, and quantization with compression plus full-precision rescoring. All of them are statements about your data, which is why recall must be measured against exact ground truth — including filtered recall, because filters, tenancy, deletes, and churn are exactly where approximate indexes quietly degrade.

The remaining discipline is operational. Choose a multi-tenancy model deliberately and enforce isolation structurally so a coding slip isn't a breach. Treat the index as derived data with a lifecycle: idempotent, version-checked synchronization from the source, tombstones and compaction, retention and genuine erasure, and a durable embedding lake so a rebuild doesn't mean re-buying every embedding. Treat the embedding spec as part of every vector's identity, and change it with blue/green indexes or named vectors, never by mixing spaces. Run migrations by copying vectors, dual-writing, backfilling resumably, shadow-reading, and cutting over gradually with a rollback window. Tune by building the measurement harness first and changing one lever at a time — memory fit, runtime knobs, dimensions, quantization, payload size, caching, replicas — always reading recall and latency together. And secure the store like the sensitive-data system it is: private networking and identity authentication, split read/write/admin credentials, access filters inside the query plus authorized hydration, typed and escaped filters, request caps, provenance controls against poisoning, encryption, and audit logs. Do the capacity arithmetic early, keep the engine behind an interface you control, and a vector database stops being a black box that is fast in demos and fragile in production, and becomes a component you can size, tune, secure, evolve, and trust.

Found this useful? Feel free to star the repo, open an issue with corrections, or share the "recall looked perfect until we turned on the tenant filter" story that made the case for measuring filtered recall click better than any benchmark chart.

articles.title: Matita 0.4.0: 60 new icons, and one number from sketchy to exact
articles.description: Matita is a set of pencil-style icons for the web, drawn by code. Lines run a little past their ends,...
articles.body_html:
Matita is a set of pencil-style icons for the web, drawn by code. Lines run a little past their ends, box corners cross, circles overlap where the pen closes. 0.4.0 is out today: 60 new icons (200 to 260) and a new setting called wobble that goes from the full sketchy hand all the way down to exact shapes.

If you haven't seen it, the first post explains the engine: [LINK to the first dev.to article]. The short version is that every icon is a line of plotted shapes, and a small deterministic engine adds the pencil habits, so the same name always draws the same way. This post is about what changed.

60 new icons, mostly what people asked for

When I posted the set, the most concrete request in the comments was a medical and science set. So that is the biggest group: 22 icons.

stethoscope, syringe, pill, test-tube, microscope, thermometer, heart-pulse, medical-cross, bandage, radiation, x-ray, dna, atom, brain, tooth, bone, ambulance, hospital-bed, mars, venus, face-mask, pipette.

The other 38 fill everyday gaps: people and files (user-check, file-check, folder-plus, mail-open), tools, devices and places (wrench, hammer, plug, keyboard, cpu, store, car, plane), and things you reach for all the time (timer, calculator, receipt, qr-code, trophy, percent, shuffle, repeat).

Every glyph still goes through the same checks: a contact sheet at 96 px and at 24 px, a bounds check with the stroke included, and a lint. That caught real things. A fingerprint read as wifi at 24 px, so it is not in the set. Six of the new icons (brain, x-ray, microscope, pipette, wrench, car) were drawn twice because the first version did not read: the first brain looked like a butterfly, so it is now a top view with two hemispheres; the first car could have been a bus, so it has a sloped roof and bigger windows now.

Not in this release: Greek letters, a lab coat and a surgeon. I couldn't draw them clearly at 24 px yet. If you need them, say which ones.

Wobble: one number, from sketchy to exact

The part I wanted most is the setting. The sketchy default is the point of the set, but there are places where you want the same icon calmer, or exactly straight.

import { SketchIcon } from '@matita/icons/react';

<SketchIcon name="wrench" />              // the full hand (default, wobble 1)
<SketchIcon name="wrench" wobble={0.4} /> // a calm hand
<SketchIcon name="wrench" wobble={0} />   // exact shapes

)

Plain JavaScript works too, and so do your own glyphs:

import { drawIcon } from '@matita/icons/engine';
import { toSvg } from '@matita/icons';

toSvg(drawIcon('calendar', { wobble: 0 }), { size: 24 });

How it works

Every habit of the pencil in the engine already had an amount: how far a line overshoots its end, how much it bows, how much a point jitters, how far a ring overlaps. Wobble multiplies those amounts:

const K = wobble, S = v => K === 1 ? v : v * K;
const j = a => (r() * 2 - 1) * a * K;          // jitter
const e1 = S(ov) * (.45 + r() * .9);           // overshoot

Two things follow from that. First, at wobble = 1 every expression multiplies by nothing, so the default draws exactly what 0.3.0 drew. I checked it with a hash over 200 glyphs at 6 seeds before and after the change: identical. Second, the random numbers come from the same stream whatever the wobble is, so 0.5 is the same drawing as 1, just calmer, not a different one. Sliding the number looks like one icon relaxing instead of flickering between takes.

At wobble = 0 the engine takes a different path: it stops sketching and draws the shapes as they are plotted. True lines, circles and ellipses as two arcs, arcs, curves, and closed shapes with square corners. There is no jitter left, so an exact icon does not depend on the seed.

Exact icons are also small. An average exact SVG is about 0.47 KB raw (0.26 KB gzipped), against about 0.82 KB (0.45 KB) for the sketchy one. There are ready-made files for all 260 at @matita/icons/exact/<name>.svg, so you can use them without running any code. The pencil variant also works over exact shapes.

Try the slider on matita.dev: there is a Wobble slider and a Perfect button next to the seed, and the copy snippets follow.

Also new on the site

  • matita.dev/changelog/ says when each icon arrived, and the icon browser shows an "Added in" label with a New badge on the latest ones.
  • matita.dev/roadmap/ is the public list of what is shipped, what is being built and what is next. Targets move.
  • matita.dev/llms.txt and matita.dev/icons.json list every icon with the version it arrived in, so an assistant (or a script) can check that a name exists instead of guessing.

Using it 

npm i @matita/icons

React components, plain SVG files, a script tag, a sprite and the Figma file are all there. It is MIT, free for personal and commercial projects, no signup. The Figma file is at https://www.figma.com/community/file/1688850201209755442 <!-- publish the Figma update to 260 icons before posting -->.

What's next

On the roadmap: search by meaning (type "delete", find the bin) targeted for November, and more science glyphs for December depending on requests. If an icon you need is missing, open an icon request. New glyphs are a line of shapes each, so they're quick to add, and 0.4.0 is mostly proof of that: 60 of them came from one list.
