articles.body_html:
Every slicer has a moment where it pops up "this model has errors" and offers to fix them. Most of the time you click yes, the print comes out fine, and you never think about it again. But when the auto-fix guesses wrong (a vent sealed shut, two parts fused, a wall that just isn't there), it helps to know what the slicer was actually complaining about.

The good news: the checks behind those warnings are simple. You can reason about them with nothing more than a list of triangles.

An STL is just triangles

An STL file has no curves, no units, and no idea which triangles belong together. It's a flat list of triangles, each with three corner points and a normal. Even the corners aren't shared: if six triangles meet at one point, that point is written six times.

That last detail matters, because every check below is about how triangles connect, and the file doesn't store connections at all. You have to rebuild them.

Step 1: weld the duplicate corners

Before you can ask "which triangles share this edge?", you need to know which corners are the same point. The usual approach is to round each coordinate to a tolerance and treat matching positions as one vertex:

// positions: Float32Array, 9 numbers per triangle (3 corners × xyz)
const TOL = 1e-6;
const ids = new Map();
const key = (x, y, z) =>
  `${Math.round(x / TOL)},${Math.round(y / TOL)},${Math.round(z / TOL)}`;

const index = [];
for (let i = 0; i < positions.length; i += 3) {
  const k = key(positions[i], positions[i + 1], positions[i + 2]);
  if (!ids.has(k)) ids.set(k, ids.size);
  index.push(ids.get(k));
}
// index now has 3 vertex ids per triangle

Welding doesn't change the shape. It only recovers the topology the format threw away.

Step 2: count how many triangles use each edge

With shared vertex ids, every triangle has three edges, and an edge is just a pair of ids. Sort the pair so A–B and B–A are the same edge, then count:

const edgeUse = new Map();
for (let t = 0; t < index.length; t += 3) {
  const [a, b, c] = [index[t], index[t + 1], index[t + 2]];
  for (const [u, v] of [[a, b], [b, c], [c, a]]) {
    const e = u < v ? `${u}_${v}` : `${v}_${u}`;
    edgeUse.set(e, (edgeUse.get(e) || 0) + 1);
  }
}

Now the three classic problems fall out of that one map.

The three things your slicer is warning about

1. Holes (boundary edges). An edge used by exactly one triangle is on the rim of an opening. A closed shell has none. A model straight out of a sculpting app with an unfinished base, or a scan that missed the underside, will have a whole loop of them.

2. Non-manifold edges. An edge used by three or more triangles. Picture two boxes that touch along one edge, or an internal wall left over from a boolean. The slicer can no longer tell which side is inside, which is where missing walls and odd infill come from.

3. Degenerate triangles. Triangles with (near) zero area: two corners in the same spot, or all three in a line. They're usually harmless leftovers from exports, but they can trip up the edge analysis and some slicers' repair passes.

"Watertight", in the sense slicers mean it, is simply: every edge is used by exactly two triangles.

What a basic repair can safely do, and what it shouldn't

Some fixes are safe because they don't invent geometry:

  • Weld near-duplicate vertices (same shape, cleaner data)
  • Drop zero-area triangles
  • Recompute normals so the preview shades correctly

Filling holes is different. A fill has to make up surface that isn't in the file, and an automatic fill has no idea whether that opening was a mistake or a vent you meant to keep. That's a decision for a tool where you can see and undo the result: your slicer's repair, Blender's fill on a boundary loop, or Meshmixer.

There are also problems an edge count simply can't see: triangles that pass through each other without sharing an edge (self-intersections), and a shell whose triangles are wound inside-out. If a model passes the edge test and still slices strangely, those are the next suspects.

Trying it on your own file

If you'd rather not write the script, I put this exact check in a browser page: STL repair check. It counts holes, non-manifold edges, degenerate triangles and duplicate vertices, runs the safe basic repair above, and gives you a repaired STL. The file is parsed in the tab and never uploaded. It deliberately does not fill holes, for the reason above.

One related trap: if your file is huge because of triangle count rather than detail, slicing is slow and repair tools choke. Reducing the triangle count first, then running the check, is often the faster path. Decimation can open small gaps, so check after reducing, not before.

Quick reference

Edge used by… Meaning Usual cause
1 triangle Hole / open boundary Unfinished base, scan gap, deleted face
2 triangles Normal, watertight —
3+ triangles Non-manifold Touching parts, leftover internal walls

If you've ever had a slicer "fix" eat part of a model, I'd like to hear what the original problem turned out to be. Did the repair check agree with your slicer?

articles.title: 90% of the AI Agents Clients Ask For Are Just a Cron Job and One API Call
articles.description: A founder asked me to build an autonomous AI agent that monitors their reviews around the clock.  I...
articles.body_html:
A founder asked me to build an autonomous AI agent that monitors their reviews around the clock.

I nodded, asked what the agent should actually do, and listened.

Every hour, someone needs to read the new Google reviews. The negative ones must reach the founder fast. That is the whole job.

Here is what I shipped.

A cron job. One LLM call per review. A Slack webhook.

That is it. No agent framework. No elaborate reasoning loop. No vector database. No memory store.

Every hour, the job pulls reviews posted since the last run. Each review goes to the model exactly once with one instruction: summarize this and flag it if it is negative. The negative ones land in the founder's Slack channel. Everything else gets logged and ignored.

It runs perfectly, costs almost nothing, and the founder loves it.

The whole system

One cron line:

0 * * * * /usr/bin/node /home/app/review-watch.js

One small script:

// review-watch.js: read new reviews, flag the bad ones, ping Slack
import OpenAI from "openai";

const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function main() {
  const since = new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();
  const reviews = await fetchNewReviews(since); // your reviews API here

  for (const review of reviews) {
    const verdict = await openai.chat.completions.create({
      model: "gpt-4o-mini",
      messages: [
        {
          role: "system",
          content: "Classify this review as positive, neutral or negative. Reply with one word, then a one line summary.",
        },
        { role: "user", content: review.text },
      ],
    });

    const [label, summary] = verdict.choices[0].message.content.split("\n");

    if (label.trim().toLowerCase() === "negative") {
      await postToSlack(`Negative review from ${review.author}: ${summary}`);
    }
  }
}

async function postToSlack(text) {
  await fetch(process.env.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ text }),
  });
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

Two moving parts. You can read the entire system in one sitting.

Why this beat the agent

An agent would have added a planning loop, tool definitions, retry orchestration and state management. For what? The input is fixed: new reviews. The schedule is fixed: every hour. The output is fixed: a Slack message for the bad ones. There is no branching decision to make, no tool to choose, no memory to carry between runs.

Every layer an agent adds on top of that is a layer you get to debug at 3am. A script fails in obvious ways: the cron log tells you exactly which line broke. An agent fails in interesting ways: a tool call went sideways three steps deep inside a reasoning chain and nobody can reproduce it.

Selling an agent when a script would do is how projects get slow and expensive.

The honest framework

Build the agent when the job has real decision making:

  • The system must choose between tools based on what it reads
  • The path branches on intermediate results, not on fixed rules
  • It needs memory across steps to finish a single task
  • The input is ambiguous enough that one fixed prompt cannot handle it

Ship the script when the job looks like this:

  • It runs on a schedule or on a trigger
  • The inputs are known and the outputs are known
  • The model does one well defined thing, like classify or summarize
  • You can read the whole system in one file

Most of the agent requests I get land in the second list. That is not a failure of ambition. It is good engineering: the simplest system that does the job.

One note on cost

This runs one small model call per review, once an hour. There is no framework overhead, no repeated reasoning passes, no state store to maintain. The bill is a rounding error and the founder has never once asked what it costs. Compare that to an agent looping through a large model for the same hourly job and the difference pays for itself.

What is the most overbuilt "AI agent" you have seen? Or built? Drop it in the comments.

I'm Sohail Khan, a Senior Full Stack Developer building AI agents and automation. Tech Lead at LoopxCorp. I write about backend engineering, AI integration and practical system design.

articles.title: Add On-Device Summarization to React with Chrome's Summarizer API
articles.description: A travel brief often mixes the trip itself with meeting context, preferences, and unresolved...
articles.body_html:
A travel brief often mixes the trip itself with meeting context, preferences, and unresolved decisions. A short summary can help the person review it before requesting proposed form changes.

That is a useful place for Chrome’s Summarizer API: a bounded reading aid beside an existing text field.

In Trip Workbench, the public demo I built and maintain, the original brief already feeds a separate Gemini feature that proposes trip fields for review. The local summary has a different purpose. It helps the person read the brief; it does not update the trip, replace the source text, or decide which details the cloud model receives.

This walkthrough builds on commit 4b3f370. The demo has the basic API call. The lifecycle extensions below add capability states, download feedback, cancellation, and a boundary that prevents an old summary from appearing beside a changed brief.

Choose a reading task with a clear boundary

Consider this synthetic brief:

I need to attend a customer workshop in New York on November 12–13, 2026. Depart SFO for JFK on November 11. Economy, one traveler. Do not book a hotel because I will stay with family. Travel only if the client confirms the workshop by Friday. Plan to return November 14, but November 15 is still possible if the workshop extends.

A useful summary would preserve the dates, the hotel exclusion, the confirmation condition, and the uncertainty around the return. A fluent summary that converts those details into a confirmed itinerary would be misleading.

Keep the original visible beside the output. Label the result “Summary of this brief” and let the person regenerate it after editing.

Continue sending the original brief to Gemini when the person selects “Suggest trip details.” Using a lossy summary as the extraction input would make any omitted condition harder for the next step to recover.

The feature needs no application API key or @google/genai call. Chrome supplies the on-device model. Chrome documents that model use does not send the input to Google or a third party, while initial model setup can require a download. That statement applies to the local inference path; the application’s separate Gemini request remains a cloud operation. See Chrome’s Summarizer guide.

Treat availability as part of the interface

Chrome documents Summarizer support from version 138, subject to platform, hardware, storage, and model availability. It remains a limited-availability web API, so browser version alone is insufficient. Serve the feature in a secure context and retain the ordinary text workflow.

There are two checks: whether the API exists, and whether it can support the configuration you want.

Use the same core options for checking availability and creating the instance. This example requests English key points in plain text. The existing demo uses a short tldr; medium key points give this review task more room without guaranteeing that every detail survives.

The examples use JavaScript and JSX. For TypeScript, Chrome recommends @types/dom-chromium-ai. Replace the demo’s handwritten Summarizer global declaration if adopting those types.

In summary-client.js:

export const summaryOptions = {
  type: "key-points",
  format: "plain-text",
  length: "medium",
  expectedInputLanguages: ["en"],
  outputLanguage: "en",
};

export async function checkSummaryAvailability(API = globalThis.Summarizer) {
  if (!API) return "unsupported";
  try {
    const value = await API.availability(summaryOptions);
    return ["available", "downloadable", "downloading", "unavailable"].includes(value)
      ? value : "unknown";
  } catch {
    return "error";
  }
}

Map the availability result to a useful UI state:

State What the interface should do
Checking Keep the brief editable while checking support
Unsupported or unavailable Explain that on-device summarization cannot run here
Downloadable Offer the action and explain that model setup may require a download
Downloading Offer to wait for readiness and show progress once attached
Available Offer summarization immediately
Unknown or error Offer a readiness retry and preserve the brief

Run this capability check in a parent Effect with a cleanup guard so a late result cannot update an abandoned panel. Do not call create() from that Effect.

Chrome’s setup guidance requires user interaction when model downloads are needed. Let the Summarize button call creation directly. Separating the readiness probe also keeps a potentially slow check out of the click path.

Availability can change. A successful probe is not a reservation; creation still needs error handling. When the language or summary configuration changes, check the new options again.

Own the summarizer for one request

For this occasional button action, one instance per request keeps resource ownership straightforward. Create it, generate the summary, and release it in finally.

Add this function to the same module:

export async function summarizeBrief(
  brief,
  { signal, onUpdate = () => {} },
  API = globalThis.Summarizer,
) {
  signal.throwIfAborted();
  if (!API) throw new Error("On-device summarization is unavailable.");
  if (!brief.trim()) throw new Error("Enter a brief first.");

  let session;
  try {
    session = await API.create({
      ...summaryOptions,
      signal,
      monitor(monitor) {
        monitor.addEventListener("downloadprogress", event => {
          if (!signal.aborted) onUpdate({
            phase: "downloading",
            percent: Math.round(event.loaded * 100),
          });
        }, { signal });
      },
    });
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    onUpdate({ phase: "summarizing" });
    const text = await session.summarize(brief, { signal });
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    return text;
  } finally {
    session?.destroy();
  }
}

The signal goes to both create() and summarize(). Cancelling while creation is pending must reach that operation, too. Aborting a creation signal after it resolves also destroys the resulting instance, so this signal belongs to this one request.

The final abort check prevents a late result from being accepted after cancellation. The finally block releases any instance that was acquired, including when generation fails.

Download progress and generation are separate phases. The Writing Assistance API specification defines download progress as a fraction with a total of 1. A displayed 100% means the download stage reached completion; the interface should still wait for instance creation and summarization to finish.

Destroying an instance releases its resources. It does not mean that the browser removes its downloaded model, nor does this code promise to cancel a shared download for every other page.

Batch output keeps this first implementation small. Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness for longer output, but it also requires managing incomplete text and clearing partial results when the request becomes stale.

Bind the result to the brief that produced it

The current demo creates an AbortController inside its click handler but does not retain it for cancellation. It also stores the resulting text without binding it to a brief version.

A person can therefore edit the brief while a summary is running, or start another request before the first finishes. The last response to arrive can overwrite the display even when it belongs to older input.

A dedicated summary component can own one active controller. This hook cancels earlier work and accepts updates only from the currently active request:

import { useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";
import { summarizeBrief } from "./summary-client.js";

export function useBriefSummary(brief) {
  const active = useRef(null);
  const [view, setView] = useState({ phase: "idle" });

  useEffect(() => () => {
    active.current?.abort();
    active.current = null;
  }, []);

  function cancel() {
    active.current?.abort();
    active.current = null;
    setView({ phase: "cancelled" });
  }

  async function start() {
    active.current?.abort();
    const controller = new AbortController();
    active.current = controller;
    const isCurrent = () =>
      active.current === controller && !controller.signal.aborted;

    setView({ phase: "preparing" });
    try {
      const text = await summarizeBrief(brief, {
        signal: controller.signal,
        onUpdate(update) {
          if (isCurrent()) setView(update);
        },
      });
      if (isCurrent()) setView({ phase: "done", text });
    } catch (error) {
      if (active.current !== controller) return;
      setView({
        phase: controller.signal.aborted ? "cancelled" : "error",
        message: error?.name === "QuotaExceededError"
          ? "This brief is too long. Choose a smaller section."
          : "Could not summarize on this device. Try again or keep reading the brief.",
      });
    } finally {
      if (active.current === controller) active.current = null;
    }
  }

  return { view, start, cancel };
}

The hook controls request ordering within one mounted summary component. Bind that component’s identity to the source so an edit also clears an already completed summary.

Trip Workbench already tracks briefVersion, editor generation, and session generation. Use them with the draft ID:

const summarySourceKey = JSON.stringify([
  state.sessionGeneration,
  state.editorGeneration,
  state.savedDraft?.id,
  state.briefVersion,
]);

<BriefSummary
  key={summarySourceKey}
  brief={state.brief}
  readiness={readiness}
/>

React resets component state when its key changes. That removes the previous output, and the hook’s cleanup aborts its request. Keep the textarea in the parent so typing retains focus.

Using the existing brief version also invalidates a result when the person edits and then restores the same text. If summary options become editable, include their version in this identity as well.

The availability probe can stay in the parent, since changing the brief does not change this example’s fixed language configuration.

Show useful states and preserve the source

Inside BriefSummary, call the hook and derive whether work is in progress:

const { view, start, cancel } = useBriefSummary(brief);
const busy = ["preparing", "downloading", "summarizing"].includes(view.phase);
const canRun = ["available", "downloadable", "downloading"].includes(readiness);

return (
  <section aria-label="Brief summary">
    <button
      type="button"
      disabled={!canRun || busy || !brief.trim()}
      onClick={() => void start()}
    >
      Summarize on this device
    </button>
    {busy && <button type="button" onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button>}
    <p role="status">
      {view.phase === "preparing" && "Preparing on-device summarization…"}
      {view.phase === "downloading" && `Downloading model: ${view.percent}%`}
      {view.phase === "summarizing" && "Summarizing…"}
      {view.phase === "cancelled" && "Summary cancelled."}
      {view.phase === "done" && "Summary ready."}
      {view.phase === "error" && view.message}
    </p>
    {view.phase === "done" && (
      <>
        <h3>Summary of this brief</h3>
        <p style={{ whiteSpace: "pre-wrap" }}>{view.text}</p>
        <p>Generated on this device. Check details against the original brief.</p>
      </>
    )}
  </section>
);

Place the readiness explanation and a readiness-retry button beside this control in the parent. A disabled action should have a reason the person can read.

Render the plain-text result through React text interpolation. The summary does not need HTML insertion.

Long inputs can exceed the model’s input quota. The summarize() API can reject with QuotaExceededError; the hook turns that into a request to choose a smaller section. For a document-oriented feature, measureInputUsage() and inputQuota can support an earlier check. A character count is not an exact token or quota measurement.

The fallback remains useful: the person can read and edit the original brief, then use the rest of the form. A cloud summary could be a separate action with a clear explanation that it sends the text to a server. Failure of the local path should not silently trigger that transfer.

Test lifecycle behavior and summary quality separately

The existing Summarizer unit test checks the missing-API case. That is a useful start, but it does not establish behavior during downloads, cancellation, or editing.

For the adapter shown here, eight controlled checks pass with a fake Summarizer. They cover availability states, availability errors, cancellation before creation, immediate creation in the call path, cancellation during creation, progress and input forwarding, rejected late output, and cleanup after generation errors.

These are lifecycle results. The React wiring has not been mounted in a browser during this walkthrough, and no native model output or performance measurement is claimed.

Use component tests for replacement requests, brief changes, draft changes, unmounting, and Strict Mode cleanup. Assert that an old result never appears beside a new source. Keep those tests deterministic with deferred promises.

Then run native browser checks with a small set of briefs:

Case What to inspect
First use on a supported device Readiness, download feedback, cancellation, and eventual completion
Model already ready Creation and generation latency without mixing in first-download time
Brief edited during generation Old output disappears and cannot return
Unsupported configuration A clear explanation and an intact editing workflow
Long brief A recoverable quota response with the original text retained
Travel brief above Dates, negation, conditions, and uncertainty preserved without invented commitments

For the travel brief, record whether the output preserves “do not book a hotel,” the client-confirmation condition, and the uncertain return date. These are evaluation criteria, not recorded model results.

Measure correctness alongside usefulness: how long it takes the person to review the summary and source, how often important details are omitted, and whether the summary saves effort at all. Very short briefs may be faster to read directly.

This gives the feature a clear role in the wider assistant: a local reading aid, tied to one version of the source, that leaves the original available for human review and the later Gemini proposal.

articles.title: AbortSignal.timeout() and AbortSignal.any(): Cancel Any Async Call in TypeScript
articles.description: Your setTimeout timeout gives up on the request but never stops it. AbortSignal.timeout(), any() and throwIfAborted() fix that, with no casts.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript Essentials
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your function promised to give up after two seconds, and it did. It threw a nice Error("timed out"), the caller logged it, the user saw a retry button. Meanwhile the HTTP request it was supposed to abandon kept downloading for another forty seconds, holding a socket, filling a buffer nobody would ever read.

That is what a hand-rolled timeout built on setTimeout and Promise.race does. It stops waiting. It never stops the work.

The fix has been sitting in every runtime for a while. Node.js added AbortSignal.timeout() in v17.3.0 and v16.14.0, and AbortSignal.any() in v20.3.0 and v18.17.0. MDN marks AbortSignal.any() as available across browsers since March 2024, and AbortSignal.timeout() since April 2024. Deno and Bun document both too.

Every snippet below is plain TypeScript that runs with node file.ts. Node's type stripping is on by default from v23.6.0 and v22.18.0, and stable since v25.2.0 and v24.12.0. On an older Node, use tsx. The snippets use top-level await, so run them in a folder whose package.json has "type": "module".

The setTimeout-and-a-flag version, and what it leaks

Here is the pattern you will find in a lot of codebases:

// race.ts: the hand-rolled timeout
async function getJson(url: string, ms: number) {
  let timedOut = false;
  const timer = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      timedOut = true;
      reject(new Error(`timed out after ${ms}ms`));
    }, ms);
  });
  const work = fetch(url).then((res) => {
    if (timedOut) return undefined; // too late, drop it
    return res.json();
  });
  return Promise.race([work, timer]);
}

Read it as the runtime does. Promise.race settles with whichever promise finishes first, and that is all it does. It has no way to reach into the fetch and stop it. The timedOut flag only protects your code from using a late result. The connection, the response stream and the JSON parse you skipped are still the runtime's problem.

There is a second leak in the happy path. When work wins, the timer is never cleared, so the pending setTimeout keeps the process alive until it fires, long after the response is in. A CLI built this way sits there doing nothing until the timer runs out.

Bun's own linter has a rule for the controller-plus-timer variant of this, prefer-timeout-signal, which flags an AbortController that only a setTimeout aborts.

AbortSignal.timeout(): one call, one deadline

fetch takes a signal option. Hand it a signal that aborts itself after a delay and the runtime tears down the request when the deadline hits:

// timeout.ts
try {
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/", {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
  });
  const body = await res.text();
  console.log(res.status, body.length);
} catch (err) {
  console.error("request failed:", err);
}

There is no timer to clear and no flag to check. Node's docs describe it as returning "a new AbortSignal which will be aborted in delay milliseconds" (globals docs).

The reason it aborts with matters for later. Per MDN, the signal's reason is a DOMException named TimeoutError. Deno's fetch timeout example spells out what that means for fetch: "When the deadline passes first, fetch rejects with a DOMException whose name is TimeoutError, not AbortError." A plain controller.abort() with no argument, by contrast, uses an AbortError DOMException as the reason (MDN).

Keep res.text() inside the try. The body arrives after the headers, and a slow body is exactly the case a deadline exists for.

One trap: the clock starts when you call AbortSignal.timeout(), not when you pass the signal to something. Create it per call. A module-level const DEADLINE = AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) is already aborted for every request made after the first five seconds of the process.

AbortSignal.any(): a user cancel and a deadline on one signal

Real calls rarely have one reason to stop. The user hits cancel, the server is shutting down, or the deadline passes. AbortSignal.any() takes a list of signals and returns one that aborts when any of them does. Per MDN, its reason is the reason of the first input that aborted.

// any.ts
const user = new AbortController();
process.once("SIGINT", () => user.abort());

const signal = AbortSignal.any([
  user.signal,
  AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
]);

try {
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/", { signal });
  console.log(res.status, (await res.text()).length);
} catch (err) {
  console.error("stopped:", signal.reason);
}

Press Ctrl-C during the request and the combined signal aborts with the AbortError from user.abort(). If the request is still running at ten seconds, it aborts with the TimeoutError.

This composes well with retries. Each attempt gets its own short deadline, and all of them share the user's cancel and one overall budget:

// retry.ts
async function getWithRetry(
  url: string,
  outer: AbortSignal,
): Promise<Response> {
  const budget = AbortSignal.timeout(8_000);
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const signal = AbortSignal.any([
      outer,
      budget,
      AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
    ]);
    try {
      return await fetch(url, { signal });
    } catch (err) {
      // the caller or the budget gave up: stop retrying
      if (outer.aborted || budget.aborted) throw err;
      if (attempt === 3) throw err;
    }
  }
}

const user = new AbortController();
const res = await getWithRetry(
  "https://example.com/",
  user.signal,
);
console.log(res.status);

The returned body is still bound to those deadlines. If it can be slow, read it inside getWithRetry, or the 2-second attempt timer can fire mid-download.

Notice the check inside catch. It asks the signals what happened instead of guessing from the error.

Make your own async functions cancellable

Passing signal to fetch covers the network. Your own loops, polls and multi-step jobs need to cooperate too, and signal.throwIfAborted() is the one-liner for that. It throws the signal's reason if the signal has aborted and does nothing otherwise (MDN).

The pattern: accept a signal, check it before each unit of work, and pass it down to everything that accepts one.

// poll.ts
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

type Job = { id: string; done: boolean };

export async function waitForJob(
  check: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Job>,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<Job> {
  while (true) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    const job = await check(signal);
    if (job.done) return job;
    await sleep(500, undefined, { signal });
  }
}

let calls = 0;
const check = async (): Promise<Job> => {
  calls += 1;
  return { id: "job-1", done: calls > 100 };
};

const deadline = AbortSignal.timeout(1_200);
try {
  await waitForJob(check, deadline);
} catch (err) {
  console.error("gave up:", deadline.reason);
}

Three places can stop this loop: the throwIfAborted() at the top of each iteration, the check function if it forwards the signal to a fetch, and the sleep. timers/promises accepts a signal and, when it is cancelled, rejects with an 'AbortError'.

The deadline above fires while the loop is sleeping, so the error that reaches your catch comes from the sleep. Node's errors docs say Node APIs throw "a Node.js AbortError", a regular Error with name 'AbortError' and code 'ABORT_ERR'. Its name says cancelled even though the cause was a timeout. The reliable place to look is deadline.reason.

Narrow the error without a cast

With strict on, the variable in a catch clause is unknown (useUnknownInCatchVariables, TypeScript 4.4), and err.name does not compile. The usual escape hatch is (err as DOMException).name, which compiles and lies whenever the thing thrown was a Node AbortError, a TypeError from a refused connection, or the string you passed to controller.abort("shutdown"). The reason can be any JavaScript value.

TypeScript 4.9 made in narrowing work on types that do not list the property, which is all you need to read a name safely:

// abort-kind.ts
export type AbortKind = "timeout" | "cancelled" | "other";

export function errorName(err: unknown): string | undefined {
  if (
    typeof err === "object" &&
    err !== null &&
    "name" in err &&
    typeof err.name === "string"
  ) {
    return err.name;
  }
  return undefined;
}

export function abortKind(
  err: unknown,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): AbortKind {
  if (signal.aborted) {
    const why = errorName(signal.reason);
    return why === "TimeoutError" ? "timeout" : "cancelled";
  }
  const name = errorName(err);
  if (name === "TimeoutError") return "timeout";
  if (name === "AbortError") return "cancelled";
  return "other";
}

abortKind checks the signal first. If the signal you own has aborted, its reason is the truth, whatever the error looks like by the time it bubbles up through a library or a Node timer. Only when the signal is still live does it fall back to the error's name, which covers a dependency that aborted on its own. Anything else is a real failure: a network error, a 500 you turned into an exception, a bug.

In practice the call site reads like this:

// use-kind.ts
import { abortKind } from "./abort-kind.ts";

const user = new AbortController();
const signal = AbortSignal.any([
  user.signal,
  AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
]);

try {
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/", { signal });
  console.log(res.status);
} catch (err) {
  const kind = abortKind(err, signal);
  if (kind === "other") throw err;
  console.log(`request ${kind}`);
}

The .ts extension in the import is required when Node strips types itself (Node docs).

No casts. If someone later throws a custom error class or aborts with a plain string, the code still type-checks and still lands in a sensible branch.

Where this goes wrong

A few edges worth knowing before you roll it out.

The timeout counts active time. MDN notes the timer is effectively paused in a suspended worker or while a page sits in the back-forward cache (MDN). For a browser tab that comes back from bfcache, "two seconds" means two seconds of running.

A combined signal cannot be detached. MDN says there is no way to unsubscribe the result of AbortSignal.any() from its inputs, and that a non-aborted combined signal with abort listeners stays alive while its sources do. If you add a listener, remove it when the work finishes:

// listen.ts
export function onAbort(
  signal: AbortSignal,
  fn: () => void,
): () => void {
  signal.addEventListener("abort", fn, { once: true });
  return () => signal.removeEventListener("abort", fn);
}

Call the returned function in a finally. That matters most for a long-lived signal, such as one tied to server shutdown, that thousands of requests combine with.

Code that ignores the signal keeps running. A synchronous CPU loop, a library without a signal option, or a function that forgets to pass it down will finish its work no matter what. Thread the signal through every layer you own and put throwIfAborted() between steps that do not take one.

Type checking. node file.ts strips types without checking them. When you run tsc, the declarations come from @types/node, which declares any(), timeout() and throwIfAborted(), or from the dom lib in a browser project. Set allowImportingTsExtensions (with noEmit) or rewriteRelativeImportExtensions so tsc accepts the .ts imports.

If this was useful

Most of this post is two things TypeScript Essentials spends real time on: async code that cleans up after itself, and narrowing an unknown into something you can trust without reaching for as. If the abortKind helper was the useful part, that book is the place to go next. If you already live in generics and want the type-level side, The TypeScript Type System picks up where it stops.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. Coming from Kotlin or Java, or from PHP 8+, swap in book 3 or 4 for the first one. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work.

I also build Hermes IDE (GitHub), an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools, so weigh this mention with that in mind.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: Building MachineConvert: a static site where every number has to show its source
articles.description: If you train in more than one gym, you know the problem: 60 kg on one brand's leg press is not 60 kg...
articles.body_html:
If you train in more than one gym, you know the problem: 60 kg on one brand's leg press is not 60 kg on another's. Levers, cams and pulleys change the force you actually feel, so the number on the stack doesn't carry over. I built MachineConvert to catalog strength machines across brands and to answer one question: "I lift X on this machine, what is it on that one?"

Here is how it's built, and the one rule that shaped almost every decision.

The rule: no number without a source

The rule is that every figure on the site carries a source (URL plus an exact quote), a date and a confidence level. If any of those is missing, the site says "no data" instead.

There are three confidence levels:

  • measured: a force gauge or dynamometer reading with photo or video proof
  • manufacturer: copied from an official spec page or sheet
  • estimated: calculated from lever, cam or pulley ratios, with a written method and a low/high range

One design decision followed from that. Manufacturer stack weights live on the machine record, never in the measurement data, and the comparator only uses measured or estimated force curves. A stack weight tells you what's on the pin, not what you feel in your hands. When the comparator does return a number, it is labeled with the lowest confidence of the two sides, and both machines show their own badge underneath.

Today the catalog has 24 brands, 50 product lines and 283 machines, with 353 sourced manufacturer values and 81 estimated points. There are 0 measured points so far, and the site says so. A comparator that says "No data yet" is better than one that makes up an answer.

The badges are filled pills with dark text and a distinct icon per level (check, document, ruler), so they don't rely on color alone.

A plain static site

There's no framework and no backend for the catalog. It's a static site: JSON data, a small vanilla JS app, and one prerendered entry page per route. That's 289 pages (283 machine pages plus a few others), each with its own title, description, canonical URL and JSON-LD. Structured data never contains load figures, so search snippets can't show a number without its source. The site is hosted on Vercel.

A synthwave grid in pure CSS

I wanted a Miami-at-night look: sun, mountains and a perspective grid scrolling toward you, animated on phones too. My first attempt drew the grid on a <canvas>, and Lighthouse made clear that was too slow. The second version is pure CSS, about 3 KB. The grid is a transformed, repeating gradient whose animation runs on the GPU, and one line of JS pauses it when the tab is hidden. With prefers-reduced-motion you get a static version. The technique was inspired by Jane Ori's "to the future" CodePen. I rewrote it from scratch rather than copying it, and the credit is in the repo.

The catch with a busy background is legibility. A navy layer always sits over the wallpaper, and an extra dimming layer turns on everywhere except the hero areas. A script (check-wallpaper-contrast.js) measures actual pixels behind the text. The worst case is 5.58:1, comfortably above WCAG AA's 4.5:1.

build.sh is the real product

Most of the work went into checks rather than features. ./build.sh has to be green before anything ships, and each check gets negative tests: I break things on purpose and confirm the check fails. Some of the checks:

  • Rendered figures: headless Chrome visits 341 pages and routes and makes sure every number shown on screen links back to a data record with source, date and level. It found 8,747 numbers and 0 unmarked ones.
  • Comparator engine: runs 5,518 machine pairs × 60 loads and verifies that no number appears unless both sides have a force curve.
  • Accessibility: axe-core at 1280 and 390 px across 368 page states, plus a full keyboard Tab walk. 0 violations.
  • Rendering: 30 page types at 390 and 1280 px, checking for no horizontal scroll, no clipped or overlapping text, and touch targets of at least 24 px on mobile.
  • Internal links: a crawler follows every route, asset, CSS url() and anchor. 0 broken out of 43,527 links.
  • Source links: all 360 unique source URLs in the data are fetched and the reports are dated.
  • Performance budget: guards against regressions, like a removed preload or a non-deferred script.

That pays off in Lighthouse. Mobile scores on the live site sit at 96–100 for performance and 100 for accessibility. Before I added font/JSON preloading and defer, performance was in the low 80s.

One lesson: checks need to know where they run. A coverage check read a local proofs/ folder that isn't part of the deploy bundle, and it broke the Vercel build. Now checks that need Chrome or local proofs print SKIPPED in the cloud and run fully on my machine.

Community measurements, moderated

The only way to get measured data is from people with a force gauge in a gym. There's a "Prepare a measurement" form that builds an email instead of posting anywhere. The form and the review tool share one rules file:

  • a measured entry requires an https link to proof
  • an estimated entry requires a method (at least 20 characters) and low < value < high
  • aggregated "it feels heavier" opinions are refused for now

Submissions go into a local queue (pending → accepted or rejected, final), handled with a small CLI. The queue is never deployed. Writing the moderation check found a real crash in the form, which is the best argument I know for writing checks.

i18n, tested with a fake language

The site is in English with French on the way. Every UI string (360 keys) goes through translation files, and a check enforces that English and French have the same keys, that no key goes unused and that placeholders match. To find hard-coded text, the whole site is rendered in a pseudo-locale (en-XA): 28 states and 17,733 text nodes. After fixes, no English remained outside catalog data such as brand and machine names. That pass also caught a page that declared itself French while serving English. The hreflang for French is only emitted once the translation is at least 95% complete, so search engines never get a half-empty locale.

What's next

The next step is more data, especially real measurements, plus a French version and comparison guides for common questions. If you lift in more than one gym, try the comparator on machineconvert.com and tell me where it's confusing. And if you own a force gauge, I'd love your help.

articles.title: 47-day TLS certificates are coming. Here's a single-file HTML tool to keep track of them
articles.description: In April 2025 the CA/Browser Forum voted to shorten public TLS certificate lifetimes: 200 days since...
articles.body_html:
In April 2025 the CA/Browser Forum voted to shorten public TLS certificate lifetimes: 200 days since March 2026, 100 days from March 2027 and 47 days from March 2029. A certificate you used to renew once a year will soon need renewing every few weeks.

Automation (ACME, certbot, win-acme) handles most of it. But there's always the leftover: the FortiGate VPN cert installed by hand, the Synology NAS, the Exchange server that needs a cmdlet after every renewal, the internal CA, and the auto-renewal job that silently stopped working three months ago.

CertScope is the fourth tool in the Scope family (after RackScope, SubnetScope and AssetScope): an inventory of certificates and domains in a single index.html.

What it does

  • Paste the PEM (or drop a .pem, .crt, .cer, .der) and the record fills itself: CN, SANs, issuer, dates, key type, serial and SHA-256 fingerprint. Paste a full chain and it keeps only the server certificate. Same CN, later expiry → recorded as a renewal.
  • Warning period based on the certificate's lifetime: a third of it, capped at 30 days. A 47-day cert warns 16 days ahead, a 90-day one 30 days ahead. No issue date? It estimates the lifetime from the CA/B Forum schedule.
  • Auto-renewal that isn't renewing: if a certificate marked as auto-renewed enters its warning window, it gets flagged — the renewal job is probably failing.
  • Domains with registrar and expiry, linked to the certificates that hang from them.
  • Reminders without a server: an .ics file with one event per reminder for Outlook or Google Calendar.
  • PDF report, CSV, JSON backup, undo/redo, command palette, English and Spanish.

Parsing X.509 in the browser, without a library

The page ships with a connect-src 'none' Content-Security-Policy, so no CDN and nothing leaves the machine. The certificate is read by a small DER/ASN.1 reader inside the HTML: walk the TLV structure, pull the validity UTCTime/GeneralizedTime, the subject and issuer CN, the SAN extension and the public key OID (RSA size or EC curve). The fingerprint comes from crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256"). If the pasted text also contains a PRIVATE KEY block, it's ignored and the user is warned.

What it doesn't do

It doesn't scan your network or connect to your servers — the HTML can't reach the internet by design. It doesn't renew anything either: certbot and friends already do that. CertScope tells you what needs renewing, where it's installed and who owns it.

Try it (opens with sample data): https://marcosblg.github.io/certscope/
Code (AGPL-3.0): https://github.com/marcosblg/certscope

How do you keep track of the certificates automation doesn't cover?
